- Our compiler has only part of wasm SIMD: `v128` loads, stores, bitwise
  operations, shuffles and `any_true`; loads and stores of one lane;
  splats and lane reads and writes on every shape; arithmetic,
  comparisons, `min`, `max`, `pmin`, `pmax` and `sqrt` on `f32x4`; and
  `add`, `sub`, `mul`, `eq`, `ne`, `all_true` and `bitmask` on `i32x4`. It
  has no shifts, no rounding, no conversions between float and integer
  lanes, no `lt`, `gt`, `le` or `ge` on `i32x4`, no loads that splat or
  widen, and no arithmetic on `f64x2`, `i64x2`, `i16x8` or `i8x16`, which
  have only splats and lane access, plus shuffles on `i16x8` and shuffles
  and swizzles on `i8x16`.
- A processor renders the same samples on every native tier and in the
  audio worklets of Chrome, Firefox and WebKit, the engine of Safari, with
  SIMD or without, which makes a rendered file a dependable reference for a
  test. One that calls the fused multiply-adds that `wasmSimd: relaxed`
  allows is the exception: they can round differently by platform, and
  natively it then runs only compiled; see `wasmSimd` in
  [../project/rive-yaml.md](../project/rive-yaml.md).
- A cast from a float to an integer, such as `<u32>x`, traps when `x` is
  NaN or out of range, and the trap fails the processor. A cast to an 8 or
  16 bit type checks the range of the 32 bit type of the same sign, then
  wraps, so `<u16>x` still traps when `x` is -1 or less. A delay line is the
  usual case, since its read position, the write position less the delay,
  goes negative. For a line whose length is a power of two,
  `<i32>Mathf.floor(pos) & (length - 1)` wraps a negative position instead,
  though a NaN or infinite delay still traps. Bring such values into range
  with a comparison before the cast, since `min` and `max` pass a NaN
  through.
- A raw pointer is good for one call only. Objects may move between calls, so
  take `changetype<usize>(array)` at the top of `process` and never keep it
  in a field.
- The block size is the host's. `frames` changes from call to call, up to the
  `maxFrames` that `init` was given. A core that wants fixed blocks renders
  whole blocks of its own and hands out what each call asks for.
- The sample rate is the output's, usually the device's own. Most devices run
  at 44100 or 48000 Hz, but a headset during a call can drop to 8000 and an
  audio interface can run at 192000. Read it from `init`'s `sampleRate`, or
  natively from `Audio.sampleRate()` on the main lane, rather than assuming one.
- A heavy processor on a loaded machine wants a bigger device buffer, at the
  cost of latency: `rive <dir> --audio-buffer=2048`, or `audioBuffer: 2048` in
  `rive.yaml`. Events stamped against `Audio.timeFrame` then need to be sent
  more than a buffer ahead.
- Make everything in the constructor or in `init`, and nothing in `process`.
- Pass large data, such as a sample bank or a model, as a shared `Blob` from
  `rive/shared`. It crosses by id, where an `ArrayBuffer` in the start
  argument is copied. For samples, `await source.toBlob(rate, channels)`
  decodes an audio asset on a job thread straight into one, resampled and
  mixed to what you ask for, so the processor reads interleaved f32 frames
  with `readInto`. Ask for `Audio.processorSampleRate()` and
  `Audio.processorChannels()`, what the processor's init is given, which in
  a browser is not `Audio.sampleRate()`.
  For audio too long to hold whole, `await source.stream(rate, channels)`
  decodes as it plays instead: the host keeps about half a second queued in
  a ring, topped up each frame, and the processor reads it through the
  stream's `reader` with `readInto`, which neither waits nor allocates. The
  reader's `ended` tells the end of the source from the host falling
  behind, and its `frame` says where in the source it is. `loop`, `seek`
  and `seekFrame` on the main lane steer it, and it decodes on while the
  processor holds the reader, so stopping the processor ends it. Builds
  that cannot run audio processors reject `stream()`. A blob asset is not
  one yet, and [Large data](#large-data) says how to load a large one.

Wasm has no instructions for sines, exponentials or logarithms, so
`Mathf.sin`, `exp`, `log`, `pow` and `tanh`, and their `Math` versions, run
full precision code inside the module. Compiled, `Mathf.sin` takes about 3 ns
on an Apple M4 Pro and `pow` and `tanh` about twice that; on the interpreter
each takes about 15 to 20 times as long. One call per sample costs little,
but a bank of voices, or a curve worked out for every sample, adds up. Keep
oscillator phases in turns and use a polynomial such as the one below, work
out smoothing coefficients when a knob changes rather than on every block,
and skip a compressor's `log` and `pow` while the signal stays under its
threshold. `Mathf.sqrt`, `abs`, `floor`, `min` and `max`, by contrast, are
single instructions.

<!-- as:file dsp.as -->
```as
// A sine of a phase in turns, where 1 is a whole cycle, within 7.4e-7 of
// Math.sin for about a quarter of what Mathf.sin costs compiled.
export function sinTurn(turns: f32): f32 {
    let x = turns - floor<f32>(turns + 0.5);
    let a = abs<f32>(x);
    x = copysign<f32>(min<f32>(a, 0.5 - a), x);
    let x2 = x * x;
    return x * (6.28316402 + x2 * (-41.3371429 + x2 * (81.3407669 + x2 * -70.9933929)));
}
```

A processor that is silent most of the time, such as an instrument between
notes, still has `process` called for every block, and runs its whole loop
unless it puts itself to sleep:

- While asleep, return from `process` at once. `out` arrives zeroed, so the
  block plays silence.
- Wake when the ring has records, which its `used` shows without taking
  them, or when the snapshot's `seq` has moved and its values differ from the
  ones in use. `seq` moves on every publish, even of the same values, so a
  main lane that publishes every frame would otherwise wake the processor
  after each publish. If the main lane publishes only when a knob changes, a
  moved `seq` is enough.
- Go to sleep once the tail is too quiet to hear.
- Publish meters as zero before going to sleep, or the main lane keeps
  showing the last level.
- `process` is still called while the processor sleeps, with the right
  `startFrame`, so a processor that keeps its own clock, such as a
  sequencer, takes its time from `startFrame` and wakes when its next event
  is due.

Asleep, a block reads `used` and `seq`, and decodes the knobs to compare them
only after a publish, so it costs close to what an empty processor does.

```as
import { Layout, Context } from "rive/host";
import { Audio, AudioHandle, AudioProcessor } from "rive/audio";
import { Ring, Snapshot } from "rive/shared";
import { sinTurn } from "./dsp";

export class Note {
    gain: f32 = 0;
}

export class Knobs {
    decay: f32 = 0.9998;
}

export class Meter {
    level: f32 = 0;
}

export class Inputs {
    notes: Ring<Note> = Ring.create<Note>(256);
    knobs: Snapshot<Knobs> = Snapshot.create<Knobs>();
    meter: Snapshot<Meter> = Snapshot.create<Meter>();
}

export class Pluck extends AudioProcessor<Inputs> {
    inputs: Inputs? = null;
    note: Note = new Note();
    knobs: Knobs = new Knobs();
    next: Knobs = new Knobs();
    meter: Meter = new Meter();
    knobsSeq: f64 = -1;
    asleep: bool = false;
    level: f32 = 0;
    phase: f32 = 0;
    step: f32 = 0;
    channels: i32 = 2;

    override init(sampleRate: f64, maxFrames: i32, channels: i32, inputs: Inputs): void {
        this.inputs = inputs;
        this.channels = channels;
        this.step = <f32>(220 / sampleRate);
    }

    woken(inputs: Inputs): bool {
        if (inputs.notes.used != 0) {
            return true;
        }
        let seq = inputs.knobs.seq;
        if (seq == this.knobsSeq) {
            return false;
        }
        this.knobsSeq = seq;
        inputs.knobs.latestInto(this.next);
        return this.next.decay != this.knobs.decay;
    }

    override process(out: StaticArray<f32>, frames: i32, startFrame: f64): void {
        let inputs = this.inputs!;
        if (this.asleep && !this.woken(inputs)) {
            return;
        }
        this.asleep = false;
        inputs.knobs.latestInto(this.knobs);
        while (inputs.notes.receiveInto(this.note)) {
            this.level = this.note.gain;
        }
        let channels = this.channels;
        for (let i = 0; i < frames; i++) {
            let sample = sinTurn(this.phase) * this.level;
            for (let c = 0; c < channels; c++) {
                out[i * channels + c] = sample;
            }
            this.phase += this.step;
            this.phase -= floor<f32>(this.phase);
            this.level *= this.knobs.decay;
        }
        this.asleep = this.level < 1e-5;
        this.meter.level = this.asleep ? 0 : this.level;
        inputs.meter.publish(this.meter);
    }
}

export class Plucking extends Layout {
    inputs: Inputs = new Inputs();
    knobs: Knobs = new Knobs();
    pluck: AudioHandle? = null;
    level: f32 = 0;
    frame: i32 = 0;

    override init(context: Context): bool {
        this.pluck = Audio.start(() => new Pluck(), this.inputs);
        return true;
    }

    override advance(seconds: f64): bool {
        // Published every frame, as a tuning panel might.
        this.inputs.knobs.publish(this.knobs);
        this.frame++;
        if (this.frame % 200 == 2) {
            let note = new Note();
            note.gain = 0.3;
            this.inputs.notes.send(note);
        }
        let meter = this.inputs.meter.latest();
        if (meter != null) {
            this.level = meter.value.level;
        }
        return true;
    }
}
```

## What each lane can reach

A lane module is compiled from the same files as the main module, but only
the code the lane's function or class reaches goes into it, and none of the
files' top level code runs there. A global the lane reads keeps its
initializer, so give state its value where it is declared. A top level
statement that changes such a global fails the build, in any script, whether
or not the script holds lane code. So does an initializer that changes one
when the lane never reads the global or static field it initializes, as the
main module runs it at start, or for a `@lazy` global once its code reads it.
The check follows the calls that code makes: into functions, methods,
constructors and field initializers, default arguments, getters and setters,
operators, and through a base class or an interface into every override, as
well as into a callback it passes straight to a call that runs it. It also
follows the global's object when code reaches it another way: through a cast,
`!`, a comma or either side of `?:`, a cascade, a local or another global set
from it, a loop over an array that holds it, a `ref` parameter, or a view over
its buffer. A standard library method counts as a change unless it only reads,
like `includes` or `slice`. When a function that code calls makes the change,
the error names it. A change made through an object a function returns gets
past the check, and so does one made through a function value, such as a
callback kept in a variable or an array and called later, or inside your code
that the standard library calls on its own, such as a map key's `hash`.

A change the main lane makes later, in a function it runs, never reaches a
lane either, since each lane starts from fresh globals. Where a function the
lane does not run itself changes a global the lane reads, the build warns
(W3011) at the function's first change to it, unless the lane changes that
global too, as it would a scratch buffer. Pass the value to the lane as an argument instead.

| Lane | Can reach |
|---|---|
| main | everything: the host, the artboard, other lanes |
| job | its arguments, shared memory, pure std code, console logs and timers, and `clock()` |
| worker | the same as a job, plus awaits on signals, ports and sleeps |
| audio processor | its argument, shared memory without locks, pure std code and console logs, but no timers |

No lane but the main one reaches the host: no paths, paints, artboards, view
models or randomness, and no other lanes. A lane that would reach one fails
the build at the call that reaches it, naming the chain of functions from the
lane's function to that call. Jobs and workers can read `clock()` to time
their own work; a job whose result depends on it no longer answers the same
on every run. In a browser each lane's clock counts from its own start, so use
it for durations.

A lane's console lines show where the main lane's do, but not at once. They
are handed over at the host's next poll, which runtimes make before each
advance, or sooner when the main lane joins the lane, releases it, or reads
its state once it is over, as `running` and `peek` do. Natively rive-cli also
hands them over once the main lane has gone about half a second without a
poll, so a main lane stuck waiting on a lane still shows what the lane logs.
`rive <dir> --test` hands them over as each case ends, so a line a lane
writes after its case has ended prints after a later case, or not at all
after the last one. A line longer than 1024 bytes is cut. Between two
handovers a worker keeps about 64 KB of lines and a job or an audio processor
about 8 KB; a lane that writes more loses the rest, and the next handover
says how many lines it dropped.

What each lane may create:

| Lane | May create |
|---|---|
| main | any shared object, and start jobs, workers and processors |
| job | blobs only, such as a large result |
| worker | any shared object; it belongs to the script that spawned the worker |
| audio processor | nothing |

## What crosses between lanes

The arguments of `Jobs.run`, `Worker.spawn` and `Audio.start`, a job's result,
a worker's resolved value, and every message through a ring, snapshot or port
cross as deep copies. These types can cross:

- numbers, bools and strings
- `ArrayBuffer`, typed arrays, `Array` and `StaticArray` of crossing types
- your own classes whose fields all cross, field by field
- the shared memory handles below, which cross as the id of the same object
  rather than a copy

Your own classes need no decorator. An object crosses as the class its type
names, so sending a subclass where its base is declared throws; send it as its
own type. Functions, host objects and values nested too deep cannot cross,
and the build says which field is at fault.

The decorators:

- `@job` marks a function `Jobs.run` may run. It must be exported under its
  own name, not generic, not a generator, and return a value.
- `@worker` marks an async function `Worker.spawn` may spawn. It must be
  exported under its own name and not a generator.
- `@sendable` marks the std types that cross by id, such as `Ring`, `Blob`
  and `Port`. You do not write it on your own classes.

## Shared memory

Shared objects live outside every lane's memory, in the host, and each lane
reaches them by id. None of them ever makes a lane wait, except a region's
lock, which audio processors cannot take, and the two bounded waits only
the main lane has.

| Type | What it holds | Who waits |
|---|---|---|
| `Blob` | bytes fixed once made | nobody |
| `SharedRegion` | bytes behind one lock, plus atomic words | a lane taking the lock |
| `Ring<T>` | values in arrival order, up to a byte capacity (4096 by default) | nobody: a full ring refuses the send |
| `Snapshot<T>` | the latest value, up to a byte capacity (1024 by default) | nobody |
| `Signal` | a counter that wakes awaits when it is notified | an await, or the main lane in `waitWithin` |
| `Port<T>` | typed messages over a ring, with awaits for a message or for room | an await, or the main lane in `receiveWithin` |
| `Barrier` | the rounds where workers splitting one computation meet, with a share of floats from each | an await, until the round's last participant arrives |

A lane holds at most one region's lock at a time, and can neither join a
job nor block on a signal while it holds one, so locks can never deadlock. A shared object holds at most
256 MB. Each handle on the main lane keeps its object alive until the handle
is collected or released; a value in flight through a ring or snapshot keeps
what it names alive until it is read or replaced.

A ring or port takes its byte capacity from the file's shared memory when it
is made, and a snapshot twice its capacity, since it keeps two copies, so a
snapshot's capacity is at most 128 MB. A value counts its encoded size
against the capacity. Today that is its encoded bytes, plus 4 for each shared
object it names and 4 more when it names any, and in a ring or port 4 more for
its length, so an `f64` needs a ring of 12 bytes. The encoding belongs to the
bake that made the file, and a later bake may size values differently, so
leave a capacity some room rather than sizing it to the byte. A value that
needs more than the capacity never fits: a ring's `send` answers false, a
snapshot keeps its last value, a port's `post` throws, and the console warns
the first time it happens, except on an audio processor. Send such data as a
blob instead, as [Large data](#large-data) shows.

A blob, or a region under its lock, moves bytes in and out by range, so
nothing needs a slice or a staging buffer first:

- `Blob.from(buffer, byteOffset, byteLength)` copies part of a buffer. The
  length defaults to the rest of the buffer.
- `Blob.fromArray(values, offset, count)` copies part of a typed array, or of
  an `Array` or `StaticArray` of numbers, counted in values, so what a job
  builds becomes a blob in one copy, or two on the web, which stages the
  bytes first.
- `blob.readInto(srcOffset, out, dstOffset, count)` copies into part of `out`,
  which is an `ArrayBuffer` or one of the arrays `Blob.fromArray` takes, and
  answers how much it copied, fewer where the blob ends first. `srcOffset`
  counts bytes in the blob, while `dstOffset`, the count and the answer count
  bytes in a buffer and values in an array. The count defaults to the rest of
  `out`.
- `view.readInto(offset, out, dstOffset, count)` and
  `view.writeFrom(offset, values, srcOffset, count)` copy between a region
  and the same buffers and arrays. `offset` counts bytes in the region, while
  the other offset and the count count bytes in a buffer and values in an
  array. The copies allocate nothing, though each `exclusive` still makes its
  view.
- `buffer.updateFromBlob(dstOffset, blob, byteCount, srcOffset)` uploads a
  blob's bytes to a `GPUBuffer`. The host copies them straight from shared
  memory, so they never pass through the script's own memory, and the blob
  may be released as soon as the call returns.
- `GPUBuffer.fromBlob(usage, blob, immutable, byteCount, srcOffset)` makes a
  buffer from a blob's bytes the same way, so a mesh that never changes can
  be an `immutable` buffer. Updating a mutable buffer while a draw still
  uses it is safe, since that draw keeps the bytes it was given.

```as
import { Layout, Context } from "rive/host";
import { GPUBuffer } from "rive/gpu";
import { BufferUsage } from "rive/gpu_enums";
import { Job, Jobs } from "rive/jobs";
import { Blob } from "rive/shared";

const kVertexBytes: i32 = 4096;

@job export function skin(pose: Float32Array): Blob {
    // Sized for the worst case; only what was written is sent.
    let vertices = new Float32Array(2 * kVertexBytes / 4);
    for (let i = 0; i < kVertexBytes / 4; i++) {
        vertices[i] = pose[i % pose.length];
    }
    return Blob.from(vertices.buffer, 0, kVertexBytes);
}

export class Skinned extends Layout {
    vertices: GPUBuffer? = null;
    skinning: Job<Blob>? = null;

    override init(context: Context): bool {
        this.vertices = new GPUBuffer(BufferUsage.vertex, <u32>kVertexBytes);
        this.skinning = Jobs.run(skin, new Float32Array(16));
        return true;
    }

    override advance(seconds: f64): bool {
        let skinning = this.skinning;
        if (skinning != null && !skinning.running) {
            this.skinning = null;
            let skinned = skinning.peek()!.value;
            skinning.release();
            this.vertices!.updateFromBlob(0, skinned);
            skinned.release();
        }
        return true;
    }
}
```

## Parallel calls

A parallel call runs one function on several threads at once, over the main
lane's own memory. The main lane starts it with `Parallel.run` and waits until
every part has returned. Nothing is copied: the parts read the main lane's
objects where they are. While the call runs nothing else changes the heap, so
reading it cannot race.

Use a parallel call for work that splits into independent pieces each frame,
such as physics, skinning, meshing or particles. Use a job or a worker for
work that runs longer than a frame, or beside the main lane.

```as
import { Layout } from "rive/host";
import { Parallel, Part, SharedArray } from "rive/parallel";

struct Velocity {
    x: f32 = 0;
    y: f32 = 0;
    constructor(x: f32, y: f32) {
        this.x = x;
        this.y = y;
    }
}

export class Body {
    vx: f32 = 0;
    vy: f32 = 0;
    fx: f32 = 0;
    fy: f32 = 0;
}

// Runs on every part. It reads the bodies in place and writes only out.
@parallel export function integrate(part: Part, bodies: Array<Body>, out: SharedArray<Velocity>, dt: f32): void {
    let end = part.end(bodies.length);
    for (let i = part.start(bodies.length); i < end; i++) {
        let b = bodies[i];
        out[i] = Velocity(b.vx + b.fx * dt, b.vy + b.fy * dt);
    }
}

export class World extends Layout {
    bodies: Array<Body> = [];
    velocities: SharedArray<Velocity> = new SharedArray<Velocity>(0);

    override advance(seconds: f64): bool {
        if (this.velocities.length != this.bodies.length) {
            this.velocities = new SharedArray<Velocity>(this.bodies.length);
        }
        Parallel.run(integrate, this.bodies, this.velocities, <f32>seconds);
        return true;
    }
}
```

| API | What it does |
|---|---|
| `@parallel` | Marks an exported function a parallel call can run. Its first parameter is its `Part`, and it returns nothing. |
| `@parallel.inplace` | As `@parallel`, and the function may also write numbers into heap objects. |
| `Parallel.run(fn, ...args)` | Runs `fn(part, ...args)` once per part and returns when every part has. All of its parts run at the same time, one on each thread the call gets, so they may `part.sync()`. Only the main lane may start one. |
| `Parallel.runParts(n, fn, ...args)` | The same with exactly `n` parts, for results that must not depend on the thread count. Parts beyond the threads run one after another, so `fn` may not `part.sync()`. |
| `Parallel.runUpTo(n, fn, ...args)` | As `Parallel.run` with at most `n` parts, for work too small to keep every thread busy. Its parts still all run at the same time, so they may `part.sync()`. |
| `Parallel.size()` | The most parts `Parallel.run` would use now: the threads a call may use, the main lane's included. It is 1 wherever a run would get one part. |
| `part.index`, `part.count` | Which part this is, from 0, and how many parts the call has. |
| `part.start(n)`, `part.end(n)` | This part's even share of the indexes from 0 to `n`. |
| `part.claim(n, grain)` | The start of the next unclaimed chunk of `grain` indexes, or `n` once every index is claimed. |
| `part.sync()` | Waits until every part of the call still running reaches it. Only code that `Parallel.run` or `Parallel.runUpTo` runs may sync. |
| `SharedArray<T>` | A fixed length array of numbers or of structs that parallel code may write. It is an ordinary object in the main heap. |
| `SharedList<T>` | A list of numbers or of structs that parts append to at once, up to a capacity it is made with. A push that finds it full answers false. |
| `atomicAdd`, `atomicLoad`, `atomicStore`, `compareExchange` | Atomics on the elements of a `SharedArray` of 32 or 64 bit integers. |
| `Parallel.inPart()` | True in code a parallel call runs and false on the main lane, as a constant the build folds, so shared code can keep what parts may not do out of the parts. |
| `PerPart<T>` | One object for each part, made on the main lane, which a part reads with `get(part)` and may write without racing the other parts. |
| `@parallel.shared` | Marks a module global or static field whose object the parts share safely, so writes into it do not warn. |
| `@parallel (...) => T` | A function type whose values a part may call. The build checks each function stored as one where it is stored. |

The arguments are not copied: every part reads the same objects the main lane
passed, so they may be of any type. A parallel call cannot start inside
another one.

### What parallel code may do

Parallel code may read anything: the arguments, any object they reach, and
globals. It may write the elements of a `SharedArray`, push into a
`SharedList`, and write its own locals, structs included. The build checks
everything a `@parallel` function reaches, as the parts run it, with what only
the main lane runs left out; see
[Code the main lane and the parts share](#code-the-main-lane-and-the-parts-share).
It reports each place that does something parallel code may not, and names the
calls that lead there from the `@parallel` function. Where the place is inside
the std, it reports the call into the std that leads there instead. Parallel
code may not:

- allocate: no `new`, closures, string building or array growth, even to build
  a thrown message
- grow the memory with `memory.grow`
- store an object reference into the heap
- write a global. A global that holds a number or an object is each part's
  own copy, made as the call began, so no other part would see the write. A
  struct global lives in memory that every part shares, so parts would race on
  it. Taking a `ref` to a struct global, or calling one of its methods that
  changes it, counts as a write.
- call the host, `console.log` included. The one exception is `clock()` from
  `rive/os`, so a part can time its own work.
- call `Parallel.size()`. It would answer 1 on most parts, so a part reads
  `part.count` instead.
- call a function value, such as a comparator passed to `sort`, unless its
  type is a `@parallel` function type; see
  [Functions a part may call](#functions-a-part-may-call)
- parse a float: `parseFloat`, `F64.parseFloat`, or a `parseInt` that answers
  a float, such as the global `parseInt` and `F64.parseInt`. They work in
  buffers in static memory that every part shares, so parts would race on
  them. Integer parses such as `I32.parseInt` are fine.
- start another parallel call or lock a shared region

`@parallel.inplace` code may also write numbers into heap objects in place,
such as a field of a body or an element of a typed array. Writes through a
`ref` parameter count as heap writes too, since a `ref` can point into the
heap. Two parts that write the same element or field race. The result is then
not deterministic, but no harm reaches the host. This is the contract a
`SharedArrayBuffer` has in JavaScript. The build warns where parts are sure
to share what they write; see [Each part's own objects](#each-parts-own-objects).

Even `@parallel.inplace` code may not write an element of a plain `Array<T>`,
since writing past its end makes it grow. Use a `StaticArray`, a typed array
or a `SharedArray` for elements that parts write, and a `SharedList` for
elements that parts append; see [Appending results](#appending-results).

`unsafe` `@parallel.inplace` code may also use `atomic.*` on the address of a
heap field or element, for example `atomic.or<u32>(changetype<usize>(node) +
offsetof<Node>("flags"), 1)`. A read-modify-write such as `atomic.add` or
`atomic.or` is then one step that no other part can split, as an atomic on a
`SharedArray` element is. The atomic must be the field's size, such as
`atomic.or<u32>` for a `u32` field, and the field's address must be a
multiple of that size, as a class lays out its fields; otherwise the atomic
traps.

A function that splits its work by `part.index` and `part.count` and writes
only its own share gives the same result on any number of threads.

### Code the main lane and the parts share

Code often serves the main lane and the parts alike, but some of it may only
run on the main lane, such as a callback to the host, an allocation or a log.
`Parallel.inPart()` tells the two apart. It is true in code a parallel call
runs and false on the main lane.

The build compiles a second copy of the functions that tell them apart, as
their parallel copies. In a parallel copy `Parallel.inPart()` is the constant
true, and everywhere else it is the constant false. So a branch on it drops out
of the copy that never takes it, and the build checks only what is left. A part
runs the parallel copies and the main lane runs the originals, so neither pays
for the test at run time.

```as
import { Parallel, Part, SharedArray } from "rive/parallel";

export class Contacts {
    touching: SharedArray<i32> = new SharedArray<i32>(64);
    events: Array<i32> = [];
    onTouch: (index: i32) => void = (index: i32): void => {};
}

// The main lane calls this for every contact, and so does each part for its
// share. Only the main lane records the event and calls back.
function update(contacts: Contacts, index: i32): void {
    let touching = (index & 1) == 0;
    contacts.touching[index] = touching ? 1 : 0;
    if (touching && !Parallel.inPart()) {
        contacts.events.push(index);
        contacts.onTouch(index);
    }
}

@parallel export function updateAll(part: Part, contacts: Contacts): void {
    let n = contacts.touching.length;
    for (let i = part.start(n); i < part.end(n); i++) {
        update(contacts, i);
    }
}

export function step(contacts: Contacts, threaded: bool): void {
    if (threaded) {
        Parallel.run(updateAll, contacts);
    } else {
        for (let i = 0; i < contacts.touching.length; i++) {
            update(contacts, i);
        }
    }
}
```

An `if` or a `? :` drops a branch, with the test written in place or through
`!`, `&&`, `||`, a `const` local set from `Parallel.inPart()`, or a call to a
top level `@inline` function that takes no parameters and returns it. Where
`Parallel.inPart()` settles a condition whatever its other operands hold, as
`touching && !Parallel.inPart()` is false in every part, those operands still
run, but the branch does not. Other tests keep every branch: a loop's
condition, a `switch`, a method, and a function that is not `@inline` or
takes parameters. When the build refuses code in a branch that such a test
guards, it says the test did not drop the branch.

Only the functions a parallel call reaches get a parallel copy, and of those
only the ones whose code differs: a function that reads `Parallel.inPart()`,
and a function on the way to one. Every other function is shared. A file with
no parallel call has no copies at all.

`Parallel.inPart()` answers for the function that calls it, so module code,
which only runs on the main lane, may not call it, and neither may a struct's
field initializer when module code makes the struct. Nor may a function that a
`@parallel` function value runs, since the main lane and the parts run the
same copy of it; see [Functions a part may call](#functions-a-part-may-call).

### Each part's own objects

Parts often need scratch objects to work in, such as a buffer to clip a polygon
into. An object that a module global holds is one object, which every part
would share. Two parts writing into it at once race, and the result is wrong
in ways that are hard to trace. `@parallel.inplace` code may write heap objects,
so the build cannot refuse such a write, but it warns (W3010) wherever a part
writes into an object a module global holds. It names the global and the calls
that lead from the `@parallel.inplace` function to the write. Each write warns
once, naming one global it may reach, and each function warns once for each
global, at its first such write.

```
warning W3010: @parallel.inplace collide writes into an object the global `clipBuffers` holds, which every part shares; give each part its own with PerPart, or mark the global @parallel.shared if the parts share it safely (through clipShared -> clipInto)
```

The build follows an object from the global through fields, array elements,
locals, `ref`s and what functions return, into the functions it is passed to.
A local stands for what it was last given, or, where a branch or a loop may
have given it more than one thing, for all of them: through `||`, `??`,
`? :`, a `for...of` loop, or an assignment later in a loop, which a write
earlier in the loop sees on the next pass. A write
the standard library makes for the code, such as setting an element of a
typed array, warns at the call that leads to it, as does `memory.copy` or
`memory.fill` into an object. A call through a `@parallel.inplace` function
value warns where it passes an object a global holds, since the function may
write into it. The build does not follow what a call through a function value
returns.
What the caller passes to `Parallel.run` is not a global's to the parts, so
writes into it never warn; parts that write the same element of it still
race. Writes into a `SharedArray` never warn, since that is what it is for,
and neither do writes into a part's own structs.

Parts often each write their own elements of an array of results. That is
safe in a `SharedArray`, so where the array a global holds is written element
by element, the warning says to write what each part makes into one: hold a
`SharedArray` in the global, or pass one to `Parallel.run`. A lambda stored as
a `@parallel.inplace` value that writes into an array it captured likewise
captures a `SharedArray` instead.

A local that starts as a shared stand-in and is set to the part's own object
only inside a branch stands for both, so writes through it warn even in that
branch. Declare a local of its own for the part's object where the code
writes, or mark the stand-in `@parallel.shared`.

`PerPart<T>` gives each part an object of its own. It is made on the main lane
from a function that makes one object, and a part reads its own with
`get(part)`. Writes through what `get` returns never warn.

```as
import { Parallel, Part, PerPart, SharedArray } from "rive/parallel";

export class ClipBuffer {
    points: StaticArray<f32> = new StaticArray<f32>(64);
    count: i32 = 0;
}

const clip = new PerPart<ClipBuffer>(() => new ClipBuffer());

function clipInto(buffer: ClipBuffer, x: f32): i32 {
    buffer.count = 0;
    buffer.points[buffer.count++] = x;
    return buffer.count;
}

@parallel.inplace export function collide(part: Part, xs: SharedArray<f32>, counts: SharedArray<i32>): void {
    let buffer = clip.get(part);
    for (let i = part.start(xs.length); i < part.end(xs.length); i++) {
        counts[i] = clipInto(buffer, xs[i]);
    }
}

export function step(xs: SharedArray<f32>, counts: SharedArray<i32>): void {
    Parallel.run(collide, xs, counts);
}
```

A `PerPart` makes all of its objects on the main lane, so no part ever
allocates one. When it is made, it makes an object for each part a call can
have at that time. A later call with more parts first makes the objects it
lacks, on the main lane, before any part starts. So the function that makes
an object runs inside that call: it must not throw, and a parallel call it
starts throws an error. A `PerPart` keeps an object for each part of the
largest call so far, for as long as the file runs, so make each one once, in
a module global or in an object that lives as long, rather than one for each
call. `T` is a class; a struct would be copied out of it, so writes would not
stay.

Sometimes the parts share an object safely, in a way the build cannot see.
A common case is a stand-in: a function hands back either an object to
work on or a shared empty one, and the code writes only when there is work,
such as when a count is above 0. Another is a buffer that only one part
uses. Mark such a module global or static field `@parallel.shared`, and
writes into what it holds stop warning. The mark is a promise the build takes
on trust: parts that do write the same element still race. It goes only on a
module global or a static field, and the build refuses it anywhere else, as
it refuses `@parallel` and `@parallel.inplace` on anything but a top level
function, and any other `@parallel.` name. The standard library marks its
`SharedArray` class with `@parallelShared`, which is a different mark that
user code does not use.

```as
import { Part } from "rive/parallel";

export class Manifold {
    count: i32 = 0;
    speed: f32 = 0;
}

export class Contact {
    manifolds: Array<Manifold> = [];
}

// What a contact with no manifold reads. Only manifolds with points are
// written, and this one has none.
@parallel.shared const emptyManifold = new Manifold();

function firstManifold(contact: Contact): Manifold {
    return contact.manifolds.length > 0 ? contact.manifolds[0] : emptyManifold;
}

@parallel.inplace export function relax(part: Part, contacts: Array<Contact>): void {
    for (let i = part.start(contacts.length); i < part.end(contacts.length); i++) {
        let manifold = firstManifold(contacts[i]);
        if (manifold.count > 0) {
            manifold.speed = 0;
        }
    }
}
```

### Functions a part may call

A part may not call an ordinary function value, since the build cannot see
which function it will be. A `@parallel` function type names functions a part
may call:

```as
export type Friction = @parallel (a: f32, b: f32) => f32;
```

The build checks each function stored as one where it is stored: in a field,
a variable, an argument or a return. It runs the same check as for a
`@parallel` function, and refuses each thing the function does that parallel
code may not, at the place that stores it, naming the calls in between.
A part may then call any value of the type.

```as
import { Part, SharedArray } from "rive/parallel";

export type Friction = @parallel (a: f32, b: f32) => f32;

function mixFriction(a: f32, b: f32): f32 {
    return Mathf.sqrt(a * b);
}

export class World {
    friction: Friction = mixFriction;
}

@parallel export function frictions(part: Part, world: World, a: SharedArray<f32>, b: SharedArray<f32>, out: SharedArray<f32>): void {
    for (let i = part.start(out.length); i < part.end(out.length); i++) {
        out[i] = world.friction(a[i], b[i]);
    }
}

export function setScale(world: World, scale: f32): void {
    // A lambda reads what it captured: its own copy, made here.
    world.friction = (a: f32, b: f32): f32 => Mathf.sqrt(a * b) * scale;
}
```

The rules:

- A `@parallel` function value is a function named directly or a lambda,
  written where the value is stored, so the build can check it. A value of an
  ordinary function type cannot become one, since it could hold any function.
- A lambda captures by value, as every lambda does, and may read what it
  captured but not assign to it. Every part calling it shares the lambda's
  copy, so a write there would race. Captured objects follow the rules for any
  other object the code reaches.
- `@parallel (...) => T` holds functions that write no heap objects, as a
  `@parallel` function writes none. `@parallel.inplace (...) => T` may write
  numbers into heap objects, and only `@parallel.inplace` code may call it.
  Writes into what a module global or the lambda's captures hold warn where
  it is stored. Writes into its own parameters do not, since what it writes
  into is what its callers pass; a call that passes what a global holds
  warns at that call.
- A `@parallel` function value is an ordinary function value too, so it may be
  stored as one and called on the main lane. A `@parallel` one may be stored as
  a `@parallel.inplace` one, but not the other way round.
- A function a `@parallel` value calls may not read `Parallel.inPart()`, since
  the main lane and the parts call one copy of it.
- A nullable one is written `(@parallel (a: f32) => f32)?`.

### Splitting the work

`part.start(n)` and `part.end(n)` give each part an even slice. When the work
per index is uneven, `part.claim` hands out chunks to whichever part asks
next:

```as
import { Part, SharedArray } from "rive/parallel";

// Costs more as j % 64 grows, so the work per index is uneven.
function cost(j: i32): f32 {
    let x: f32 = 0;
    for (let k = 0; k < j % 64; k++) {
        x += Mathf.sin(<f32>k);
    }
    return x;
}

@parallel export function shade(part: Part, cells: SharedArray<f32>): void {
    let n = cells.length;
    for (let i = part.claim(n, 64); i < n; i = part.claim(n, 64)) {
        let end = min(i + 64, n);
        for (let j = i; j < end; j++) {
            cells[j] = cost(j);
        }
    }
}
```

`part.sync()` splits a call into stages. Every part finishes one stage before
any part starts the next, so a stage can read what other parts wrote in the
stage before. Every part that is still running must make the same syncs in
the same order. A part may return early, for example when its share is
empty, and it then counts as arrived at every later sync, so the others do
not wait for it.

Every part claims from one shared count, which starts again from 0 after each
sync. So a stage has one claim loop, and two claim loops need a
`part.sync()` between them; otherwise a part still in the first loop takes
the second loop's indexes.

`part.sync()` needs every part running at the same time, and `Parallel.run`
and `Parallel.runUpTo` promise that. They get one part on each thread they
can use, however few that is, so their parts always run together. Where a
call gets one part, its syncs return at once. `Parallel.runParts(n)` may run
its parts one after another, so the build refuses it for a function that
reaches `part.sync()`, and names the calls in between. Staged work that needs
a fixed part count gives each stage its own `runParts` call instead, and the
end of each call is the barrier. A sync costs less than a call, so where the
part count may vary, one `Parallel.run` with syncs is faster.

Parts that write next to each other in memory slow each other down, even
without racing, as the cache line they share moves between cores. Give each
part whole cache lines, 16 floats or more, where it can.

### Appending results

Parts often find a few results among many inputs, such as the contacts that
need work later, and append them to a list. A part cannot grow an `Array`,
since growing allocates. A `SharedList<T>` is made on the main lane with room
for a number of elements, and parts push into it without allocating.

```as
import { Parallel, Part, SharedArray, SharedList } from "rive/parallel";

@parallel export function findFast(part: Part, speeds: SharedArray<f32>, fast: SharedList<i32>): void {
    for (let i = part.start(speeds.length); i < part.end(speeds.length); i++) {
        if (speeds[i] > 10) {
            fast.push(i);
        }
    }
}

let fast = new SharedList<i32>(64);

export function step(speeds: SharedArray<f32>): void {
    fast.clear();
    Parallel.run(findFast, speeds, fast);
    if (fast.overflow > 0) {
        // Room for every push, then the call again.
        fast = new SharedList<i32>(fast.capacity + fast.overflow);
        Parallel.run(findFast, speeds, fast);
    }
}
```

A push claims the next index in one step, so any number of parts may push
into one list at once. A push into a full list changes nothing and answers
false, and `overflow` counts those pushes until the next `clear()`, so the
main lane can make a list with room for them. That count covers every result
only when parts keep pushing once the list is full, as `findFast` does.
Elements are numbers or structs of numbers, as in a `SharedArray`, and
`list[i]` reads and writes the ones pushed so far.

When parts push into one list at once, the order of their elements depends
on which part got there first, so it can change from run to run. Where the
order matters, give each part its own list through a `PerPart`, where its
elements stay in the order it pushed them, or sort the list once the call
returns. Read what parts pushed after a `part.sync()` or once the call
returns, since a part may still be writing an element it claimed. Clear the
list on the main lane, or in a stage in which no other part uses it, for the
same reason.

### Failures and limits

A part that throws or traps fails the call that started it, as a throw on the
main lane would, and the other parts stop. The call reports the first
failure. A parallel call counts against the main lane's call budget. When the
budget runs out, every part stops, through the watchdog natively or through
fuel in a metered bake.

Natively `Parallel.size()` is the job pool's threads plus the main lane's, 7
on most desktops. `--job-threads=<N>` sets the job pool's threads, and so the
size as well. With the default thread count, a run also uses no more parts
than the device has fast cores, since a part on a slow core makes every sync
wait for it. This limit applies only where the system says how fast each
core is. On Apple chips the fast cores are the performance cores, for example
6 on an M5 Max. On Linux and Android, where the system reports each core's
capacity, which is mostly on ARM chips, they are the cores at least half as
fast as the fastest. Most x86 Linux machines report no capacity, so they have
no such limit, and neither does any other system. A thread count set with
`--job-threads` is used as given.

A run can get fewer parts than `Parallel.size()`, so parallel code reads
`part.count`. That happens when the host cannot start as many threads, or
runs out of memory for them, and when another file's parallel call is using
the threads, since every file shares one set. A call that finds them in use
does not wait for them. It runs on the main lane alone instead: a run as one
part, and a `runParts` call's parts one after another. A host can run
every parallel call one part at a time, on the main lane, with
`parallelSafeMode` in its limits, and rive-cli with `--parallel-safe`.
`Parallel.size()` is then 1, and so it is while a debugger is attached and in
a file's top level code, where runs get one part too.

`Parallel.runParts(n)` and `Parallel.runUpTo(n)` throw a `RangeError` when `n`
is below 1. A file keeps the `Part` objects of its largest call for as long
as it runs, so a `runParts` call with a very large `n` holds that many
objects from then on.

Natively the threads that run jobs, workers and parts each have 8 MB of
stack, as much as a main thread has on macOS, Linux and Android, so recursion
that runs on the main lane runs in every part. rive-cli gives its own main
thread 8 MB on Windows too. In any other host the main lane runs on the
host's own thread, so how deep it can recurse is the host's choice. A
Windows app's main thread gets 1 MB unless the app asks for more, and the
editor and Flutter apps keep what their platform gives them.

A file with parallel calls shares its memory between threads. The memory
starts small and grows as the main lane needs more, as any file's does, but
only between calls, which is why parallel code cannot allocate. Natively it
takes only the address space it uses, and moves when it outgrows it.
`wasmMaxPages` in `rive.yaml` caps how far it can grow; see
[../project/rive-yaml.md](../project/rive-yaml.md).

A parallel call costs very little to start. On a desktop, compiled, an empty
call costs about 0.03 µs with one part, 0.2 µs on 2 threads, 0.3 µs on 4 and
0.9 µs on 8. A `part.sync()` costs well under a microsecond. With 5 to 10 µs
of work per part between syncs, 4 parts run at about 90% of perfect scaling.
8 parts run at 60 to 85%, as each part then needs a fast core that no other
work is using.

### In a browser

A file with parallel calls loads and runs in every browser. Its calls run on
threads only on a page with cross origin isolation that loads the build of
the runtime with threads. Anywhere else, `Parallel.size()` is 1, so
`Parallel.run` and `Parallel.runUpTo` get one part each and
`Parallel.runParts(n)` runs its `n` parts one after another, all on the
page's thread.

The build with threads loads only on such a page. Anywhere else it fails to
load at once and says why. Our runtimes load their build without threads
there instead: the JS runtime's `@rive-app/webgl2-threads` package and
rive_native on the web both do.

With isolation and threads, the page starts a team of worker threads, and
`Parallel.size()` is the team plus the page's own thread. By default that
is one part for each core the browser reports, up to 8. Browsers do not say
which cores are fast, so a part can land on a slow one, and every sync then
waits for it. More parts make each part's share smaller, so a slow core
holds the others back for less time, which is why the web uses more parts
than the fast cores a native run keeps to. On an M4 Pro, with 10 fast cores
and 4 slow ones, staged work split evenly ran 1 to 28% faster on 8 parts
than on 7 in Chrome, Firefox and WebKit. Past 8 it got slower in Firefox,
and in Chrome once the parts reached the slow cores, up to several times
slower on short stages.

A page can pick the number itself, before it loads its first file. 1 turns
parallel calls off, so every call runs on the page's thread as it would
without threads.

- The JS runtime: `RuntimeLoader.setParallelParts(n)`, and `null` for the
  default.
- rive_native: `RiveNative.parallelParts = n`, and `null` for the default.
- A page that loads the runtime's module itself:
  `Module.riveScripting.parallelParts = n`.

This number is separate from the job pool. Natively one setting sizes both:
`jobThreads` in a host's `ScriptingLimits`, which rive-cli's `--job-threads`
sets, gives the job pool its threads and parallel calls one part more. On the
web `jobThreads` sizes only the threads that run jobs, so a page that sets it
still gets the default number of parts until it sets `parallelParts` too.
`parallelSafeMode` in `ScriptingLimits` runs every call one part at a time on
the web as natively.

Each team thread runs its own copy of the file's module over the same
memory. A call runs one part on the page's thread and one on each team
thread, and the result is the same as natively. A host that prepares the
file before it starts its scripts has the team ready for the first call. One
that does not gets fewer parts, down to 1, until the team is ready.

The page's thread cannot sleep, so while it waits for the other parts it
keeps checking, and so does part 0, which runs on it, at a `part.sync()`.
Natively part 0 sleeps there after a while, as every part does. The team
threads check for about 50 µs after each call, then sleep until the next
one. In Chrome and Firefox a sleeping team thread still hears about a file
loaded later. WebKit can lose the wake of that kind of sleep, so there, and
in a browser without `Atomics.waitAsync`, a team thread sleeps in a way that
a call wakes at once, and wakes every 2 ms to listen for a file loaded later.

A team thread that never starts its part does not hang the page. After a
millisecond the page wakes the team again. If the thread still has not
started, the call fails once its budget runs out, or after a second when it
has no budget, saying that a thread of the page's team did not start its
part. Part 0 checks in with the page now and then while it waits at a
`part.sync()`, so a call fails that way there too. Later calls run without
that thread until it wakes.

With isolation the file's memory is shared between threads. The browser then
sets aside room for that memory up front. The page asks for 2 GB, or for
`wasmMaxPages` if that is less, and halves the request until the device can
give it. The memory can then grow that far but no further. Without isolation
the memory is not shared, since such a page cannot share memory between
threads, and it grows as any file's memory does.

A call costs more to start on the web than natively. In Chrome on a desktop,
an empty call costs about 0.1 µs with one part and about 1 to 1.3 µs on 2 to
8 threads, against 0.03 and 0.2 to 1 µs natively. A `part.sync()` costs
about what it does natively, 0.15 µs on 2 threads and 0.5 µs on 8, so staged
work does best as one call with syncs.

A call that comes after main lane work of more than about 50 µs finds the
team asleep, and waking more threads takes longer. On an M4 Pro such a call
costs about nothing more on 4 parts than on one, and 40 to 60 µs more on 8,
in Chrome and WebKit alike. So where a frame makes a few short calls between
main lane work, `Parallel.runUpTo(4, ...)` can beat 8 parts, and work that
can share one call with syncs between its stages keeps the team awake.

## What a job costs

A job pays for its start, for copying its arguments in and its result out,
and for the wait if it finishes after the main lane needs it. On a desktop,
natively, an empty job run and joined costs about a hundredth of a
millisecond, and a megabyte crossing in or out about a few tenths. In a
browser each is a few times more. The main lane encodes the arguments inside
`Jobs.run` and decodes the result inside the call that reads it, so those
copies cost its frame; [Large data](#large-data) says how much, and how to
avoid them.

A job usually starts in the instance an earlier job of the file finished in,
reset to a fresh state, which is why its start is cheap. A job whose memory
grew past 64 MB leaves no instance behind, so the next one instantiates the
module again and touches its memory anew, about a millisecond for every 25 MB.
A host changes the size with `jobReuseBytes` in its `ScriptingLimits`; each
script module in a file keeps at most one such instance per job thread.

So a job that runs every frame pays off when its work is clearly larger than
what crosses. Half a millisecond of work that returns two megabytes is slower
on a job than on the main lane, while several milliseconds of work returning
the same amount gains. Two habits make the most of one:

- start it early and join it late: start the job as soon as its inputs are
  ready, do the frame's other work, and join just before the result is used
- send less: pass shared memory or a `Blob` rather than large arrays, and
  decode into a value you keep with `joinInto`

What crosses cheaply:

- a typed array, an `Array` of numbers or a `StaticArray` of numbers crosses
  as one block of bytes, never copied element by element, though a
  `StaticArray` always sends its whole length (see [Large data](#large-data))
- a `subarray` view sends only its own bytes, which splits work across jobs
  without copying the whole array
- a `Blob` crosses by id with no copy, and a job that returns one skips the
  copy into the main lane; read it in place with `readInto` or hand it to
  `updateFromBlob`

Keep a `Job`, `Worker` or processor handle in a field for as long as the lane
should run. A handle that is collected stops its lane, as releasing it does.

## Large data

A value that crosses is copied by the lanes at both ends. The lane that sends
it encodes it inside the call that sends it: `Jobs.run`, `Worker.spawn` and
`Audio.start` for their arguments, and `post`, `send` and `publish` for a
message. The lane that reads it decodes it inside the call that reads it:

- a job's or worker's result in the first `peek`, `join` or `joinWithin`
  that finds the lane over, or for `promise()` at the host's next poll, which
  runtimes make before each advance
- the same result again in every `joinInto` or `peekInto` that answers true
- a message in the `receive`, `drain`, `latest` or other read that takes it

So a large result costs the frame that reads it. Numbers are copied as
blocks, but every other object is made on its own:

- a typed array, or an `Array` or `StaticArray` of numbers, is one block:
  4 MB decodes in under half a millisecond
- every object, string and nested array is made one at a time: 350,000
  objects of three numbers take about 4 ms to decode compiled and about 25 ms
  interpreted
- awaited results are paced by bytes, not objects, so a few megabytes of
  small objects can still cost several milliseconds in one poll
- the first large result also grows the memory of the lane that reads it,
  which costs several times more, once
- what the main lane keeps of a result made of many objects is moved by the
  collector at the next frame, which can cost more than the decode itself

Encoding works the same way, so a large argument or message made of many
objects also costs the lane that sends it.

Measured natively on compiled code, per megabyte, a job's start and join
included:

| What crosses | Cost per MB |
|---|---|
| a typed array or an array of numbers, as an argument | about 0.06 ms |
| an array of small objects, as an argument | 1.2 to 1.4 ms |
| an array of small objects, as a result | 4.4 to 5.4 ms |
| a typed array result read with `join` | 0.8 to 1.7 ms, since the main lane allocates it |
| a typed array result read with `joinInto` | about 0.12 ms |
| a `Blob` read with `readInto` into a buffer you keep | about 0.06 ms |

So arrays of objects cost 20 to 90 times what numbers do, and a large result
belongs in a `Blob` or is read with `joinInto`.

A `Blob` crosses by id whatever its size, so reading one decodes nothing.
For large data:

- make the blob where the data is computed, in a job or a worker: build the
  numbers in a typed array, an `Array` or a `StaticArray`, then return or
  send `Blob.fromArray(values)`, which copies them once, or twice on the web
- hand a fetched body to a job as the `Blob` that `response.blob()` resolves
  with, awaited into a local first since an await cannot sit inside a call's
  arguments, rather than as an `ArrayBuffer` from `arrayBuffer()`, which
  first copies it into the lane
- publish data that every job reads, such as a style, once to a `Snapshot`
  large enough for it, and pass the snapshot, whose handle crosses by id;
  each job then decodes the data on its own thread
- read a blob without decoding it: `updateFromBlob` and `GPUBuffer.fromBlob`
  upload its bytes straight from shared memory, as the skinning example under
  [Shared memory](#shared-memory) does, and `readInto` copies just the range
  you need into a buffer you keep

A blob asset reaches the lanes through the main lane, since only the main
lane reaches the host. `context.blob(name)` copies the asset's bytes into the
main lane's memory, and `Blob.from` copies them again into shared memory. The
main lane's memory never shrinks, and a buffer it drops during a call is
reclaimed only at the next frame, so a large asset loaded whole leaves the
main lane that much bigger for good. Until the host can make a blob straight
from an asset, split a large asset into several blob assets and load one per
advance with `context.blob` and `Blob.from`, so the main lane grows by about
one part, and release each `Blob` once the workers that read it have
unpacked it.

An audio asset does not take that detour: `source.toBlob(sampleRate,
channels)` decodes it on a job thread, or a slice a frame on builds with no
job threads, straight into a shared `Blob` of interleaved f32 frames, which
never enters the main lane's memory, and its promise resolves at a later
frame. The blob holds exactly the frames that
decoded. Pass it in an audio processor's start argument and read it there
with `readInto`.

An `Array` sends its length and a typed array view only its own bytes, but a
`StaticArray` always sends its whole length, so one kept as a buffer with a
count of its own sends its capacity. Keep such a buffer as a typed array and
send `subarray(0, count)`, push into an `Array` instead, or for a large result
hand over `Blob.fromArray(buffer, 0, count)`.

Since a ring, snapshot or port holds only what fits its byte capacity, keep
messages small and send large data, such as a tile's geometry, as a blob the
message names. Post the message and release your own handle on the blob:
the message holds the blob until it is read, and the reader then holds it
until it releases it. A worker holds what it made until it releases it or
is gone, so a long lived worker releases each blob once it has posted it. A
large message also leaves the lane that sent or read it holding a buffer of
that size.

## Limits

The host that plays a file sets its limits, and content cannot change them:

- each call the host makes into the main lane, `init`, `advance`, `draw` and
  the rest, has a budget, 200 ms by default
- an audio processor has a hard limit in blocks of audio, 2 by default; a
  block past it takes that processor out of the mix, and a limit of 0 turns
  it off
- a file and its lanes hold at most 512 MB of shared memory at once by
  default, and at most 65536 live shared objects

Natively the job pool and the worker pool size themselves to the device: one
thread fewer than it has cores, at most 6 for jobs and 4 for workers. In a
browser with threads the job pool sizes itself the same way, and workers get
threads as [Platform differences](#platform-differences) says. rive-cli takes
`--job-threads=<N>` and `--worker-threads=<N>` to run a project on pools of
another size.

A file's top level code runs once, when the file loads, and it is bounded
like any call into the main lane. It has the same budget, and code that runs
past it fails the file. A join or wait there gives up when the budget runs
out, as it does in `init`, and a join then answers null while its job keeps
running. So start lanes at the top level if you like, and read their results
in `init` or later.

Jobs and workers have no time limit. A job runs until it returns or is
stopped, and a worker until its promise settles or it is stopped. The one
exception is a browser build without threads, which runs every job and steps
every worker on the page's own thread: there a job run or a worker step that
has fuel fails once it passes the main lane's call budget, as a call into the
main lane does, so it cannot freeze the page. `stop()` on a job or worker
handle always works natively, and in a browser wherever the lane has fuel, as
[Platform differences](#platform-differences) says. On a processor handle it
takes the processor out of the mix once its current block returns, fuel or
not. Releasing the handle stops the lane too.

A join never waits past the main lane's budget. It answers null while the
job is still running, and the job keeps running on the pool. Only a call
without a budget runs a job no thread has started on its own thread, to its
end.

A join or wait gives up about 20 ms before the budget ends, so the script
has time to act on the answer. One begun inside those last 20 ms only tries,
and a region lock begun there waits at most half of what the call has left.
So a loop that keeps retrying a join, a wait or a lock still runs out of the
budget, and fails the call.

## Captures

Jobs and workers run on wall time, while a headless capture steps its frames
as fast as the machine allows. Left alone, a job's result would land at a
different frame on every run. So rive-cli's `--screenshot`, `--semantics`,
`--data-dump` and `--render-audio` wait, after the load and after every frame,
until each job the scripts started has finished, their workers are idle and
their audio processors have started. What a frame starts is then always there
in the next one. `--render-audio` pulls a frame's audio only once its lanes
have settled, then waits again for any workers its processors woke while they
rendered, so what those workers send also lands in the next frame.

The capture counts the workers as idle when none of them is running a step
and none has a wait that has fired. A wait fires when its signal is notified
or its timeout passes, and a ring or port notifies its signals on every write
and every read. So:

- Workers that meet at a barrier settle together. The last one to arrive
  notifies the others during its step, so their waits have already fired by
  the time it awaits again, and the capture waits for them too.
- Stalled workers count as idle. A worker awaiting an event that never comes
  looks like one with nothing to do, so a capture cannot tell a stall from a
  finished frame.
- A worker waiting on `Worker.sleep`, or on a timed wait nothing has notified,
  counts as idle.

Timed waits follow the wall clock on both lanes, not the capture's frames.
That covers `Worker.sleep` and every await with a timeout, in a worker or on
the main lane, the main lane's own `Worker.sleep` included. A capture can step
many frames in the time a short sleep takes, so in a capture, pace lanes with
signals, ports and rings rather than with time.

A worker that fills a ring for a processor should await the ring's
`spaceSignal` when the ring is full, rather than poll it with a sleep. A
capture renders a frame's audio in one go, 800 samples per channel at 48000
Hz, so the ring should hold more than that much audio plus one record, since
a worker that waits for room can leave nearly a record of the ring empty. A
smaller ring, or a worker that polls, leaves gaps of silence that change from
run to run.

A single wait that lasts 60 seconds ends the waiting for the rest of the run.
After about 5 seconds of one wait, the log says which frame is still waiting
and on which lanes, counting the load as frame 0. When the capture gives up,
the log names the frame, and the end of the run repeats the warning, even with
`--quiet`, and exits with failure. The capture still writes its files, but
another run may not match them.

- `--no-settle-lanes` turns the waiting off.
- `--bench` never waits, and it reports what the frames cost, not what the
  lanes cost. Its jobs and workers run beside the frames it times, while its
  processors start but render nothing, since a bench plays no audio.

When a capture gives up, and when any headless run ends, the log also names
each worker still parked on an await, what it awaits and for how long, as in
`worker phase is still waiting for signal 2147487744 after 1.25 s`. A port's
messages queue in a ring, so a worker awaiting a port's `receive` waits for a
write to that ring and one awaiting `writable` for a read from it; a script
reads the ring's id as `port.ring.id`. Nothing checks whether anything could
still wake a worker, so a service waiting for its next request is named too.
The end of a run whose capture gave up repeats the workers named then after
its warning, even with `--quiet`.

## Platform differences

**Native** (desktop, mobile, consoles): modules run on WAMR. Jobs and workers
run on pool threads. A stopped job is interrupted at once, and a stopped
worker that never awaits again is interrupted after a short grace. These
interrupts reach every lane, with fuel or without, so there a lane's fuel only
costs speed. Processors run on the engine's audio thread; their `init` runs
off it. A host with no pool threads runs each queued job on the main lane's
thread at the next advance, at least one per advance and more while they are
quick, and a job run that way runs to its end.

**Web**: modules run on the browser's own wasm engine. A build with threads
loads only on a page served with cross origin isolation, the two headers a
browser needs before it shares memory between threads, so a page without them
needs a build without threads. A build with threads
runs jobs and workers on web workers. Each worker keeps the web worker it
started on for its whole life, awaits included, so up to 8 or so of a file's
workers alive at once each hold one. Past that, workers share threads, and a
step that runs long holds up the other workers on its thread. These threads
come from the pool of web workers the build starts with, and a thread past the
pool starts only once the page's thread returns to the browser. So a host
sizes that pool, emscripten's `PTHREAD_POOL_SIZE`, to hold up to 6 job
threads, one thread that schedules workers and 8 threads for each file's
workers. That makes 15 for a page with one file, besides any threads of the
host's own. A build without
threads steps workers between frames and runs each job on the page's thread at
the next advance, unless a join from a call without a budget runs it there
first, to its end.

A browser cannot interrupt a running call, so a lane ends early only at a
check of its own. A module baked with fuel asks, every so often as its loops
and calls run, whether it must end. A bake gives its job, worker and processor
modules fuel exactly when it gives its main module fuel: every debug bake
does, the web editor's previews among them, and so does an optimized bake with
`wasmFuel`; see `wasmFuel` in
[../project/rive-yaml.md](../project/rive-yaml.md). With fuel:

- a call into the main lane that passes its budget fails, as natively
- a stopped job ends at its next check, whether or not it polls
  `Lanes.stopping()`
- a stopped worker that awaits again ends at that await, and one that never
  does ends at its first check once a 50 ms grace has passed, as natively
- releasing the file ends its jobs and workers the same way, so each gives
  back the web worker it held
- without threads, a job run or a worker step that passes the main lane's
  call budget fails, as a call into the main lane would, and the page goes on
- a processor block past its hard limit ends at its next check, and only that
  processor fails; an `init` still running after a second fails the same way

Without fuel, as in an optimized bake without `wasmFuel`:

- a call into the main lane that runs past its budget is never stopped, so a
  runaway loop hangs the page
- a stopped job sees `Lanes.stopping()` turn true, and stops only once it
  polls that; one that never polls runs to its end, and without threads it
  holds the page until it returns
- a job run on the page's thread runs to its end, as the main lane's own
  code does
- a stopped worker ends at its next await, never in the middle of a step
- a processor block cannot be cut short: one past its hard limit is dropped
  once it returns, and one that stalls the audio thread for a second fails
  every processor and drops the output

Processors play in real time only in a build with threads, in an audio
worklet. Without threads a processor fails as it starts, and `failed` on its
handle says why. A processor's `init` runs in the worklet too, on the audio
render thread, so heavy setup delays the mix. A processor's `startFrame` and
the sample rate its `init` gets come from the page's audio output, whose frames
and rate `Audio.timeFrame` and `Audio.sampleRate` do not report, so a note
the main lane stamps with a frame from `Audio.timeFrame` does not play on
that frame. A browser cannot put its
page thread to sleep, so a `join`, `receiveWithin` or `waitWithin` there
spins until it is answered, for at most a tenth of a second, taking a core
the pool could use. Where the result can wait a frame, poll `running` or
await `promise()` instead. Without threads `receiveWithin` and `waitWithin`
never wait, since a worker only steps between advances. A file baked with SIMD the browser
lacks runs none of its scripts and says so on the console; see `wasmSimd` in
[../project/rive-yaml.md](../project/rive-yaml.md).

**NRDP**: as the web, except that a build with threads needs no cross origin
isolation there, and processors run on NRDP's own audio worklet thread, which
the page starts for them. A block that stalls that thread for a tenth of a
second fails every processor and ends the thread. With fuel, a block past its
hard limit ends at its next check, which at the default limit comes long
before that, so only its own processor fails. A processor's first block is
the exception: it is allowed a tenth of a second, so it can still stall the
thread.


## TOPIC: debugging

# Debugging scripts

The preview can host a debugger for the Luau and AnimaScript scripts in
a project. VS Code speaks to it through the Rive extension; any Debug
Adapter Protocol client can connect the same way.

## From VS Code

Install the Rive extension, open the project folder and press F5. The
extension runs `rive <project> --debug` in a terminal, waits for the preview
to come up and attaches. Breakpoints in `.luau` and `.as` files, stepping,
the call stack and the Debug Console work as they do for any other language;
Luau frames also show locals and upvalues and answer a hover. Script errors
pause where they were raised, with the message; turn that off under
Breakpoints, "Script errors".

To attach to a preview you started yourself, run it with `--debug`:

```bash
rive . --debug          # listens on 9641
rive . --debug=9700     # any port
```

then pick "Rive: attach to preview" from the Run and Debug dropdown, or add
the configuration to `launch.json`:

```json
{ "type": "rive", "request": "attach", "name": "Rive: attach", "port": 9641 }
```

The listener is loopback only.

## View models

The debugger shows the data the preview is bound to, whichever language
your scripts are in, and whether or not one has stopped.

- **View Models panel.** Under Run and Debug, the View Models panel lists
  the artboard's own view model instance and every global one. It refreshes
  while the preview runs, so you can watch values move. Expand a nested view
  model or a list to see what is inside it. Hover over a number, string,
  boolean, color or enum and press the pencil to change it, or press the
  bolt on a trigger to fire it.
- **At a stop.** The Variables panel adds a View Models scope beside Locals
  and Upvalues. Set Value works there too. A value you set while paused takes
  effect when you continue, and a value it cannot take is reported in the
  Debug Console then.

Values are read and written the way `--data` takes them: numbers in plain
form, colors as hex ARGB or RGB like `FF3311BB` or `3311BB`, enums by the
name of an option, and booleans as `true`, `false`, `1` or `0`. A value the
property cannot take is refused with the reason.

### Breaking when a value changes

Right click a view model value in Variables and pick **Break on Value
Change**, or press the breakpoint button beside it in the View Models panel.
The next time anything writes that value, the preview stops where it was
written.

- **A script wrote it.** The stop lands on the line that assigned it, in
  Luau or AnimaScript, with the full call stack.
- **The scene wrote it.** A listener action, or a data bind writing back to its
  view model, has no line to show. The call stack lists what did it instead,
  innermost first, for example `Bind from a listener's value`,
  `Listener 'Tap'`, `State Machine 'State Machine 1' on Artboard 'Main'`. An
  action on a state or transition names its layer too. A write from outside
  any script or state machine says so.
- **The message says what changed**, like `Main/stats/bursts: 0 → 1`, and a
  trigger says it fired.

A stop in the scene has no lines to step through, so stepping from it just
continues. Your own edits from the debugger never stop, but whatever they set
off does:
firing a trigger from the panel stops in the script listener that reacts to
it. A breakpoint follows its path, so it survives a rebuild and a script
replacing a nested view model or a list row.

## What to expect

- **Rebuilds keep the session.** Save a script and the preview rebuilds as
  usual; the breakpoints are planted again in the new build. A build that
  lands while you are paused waits until you continue.
- **Breakpoints move to the next executable line.** A breakpoint on a blank
  line, a comment or `end` binds to the next line that runs, and the editor
  shows where it landed. One that binds nowhere stays hollow.
- **The window freezes while paused.** Scripts run on the preview's own
  thread, so a stop holds the whole window, including its menus, until you
  continue. Its terminal keeps logging.
- **Stepping out of a callback lands in the next one.** Protocol methods
  like `advance` and `draw` are called from the runtime, so stepping out of
  the outermost frame stops at the first line the runtime runs next, usually
  the next callback of the frame.
- **`async` functions.** A breakpoint inside an `async` body stops on that
  coroutine, with its own stack. Stepping over a yield lands where the
  resumer continues. In AnimaScript an async body is one frame per
  resume: it leaves the stack when it suspends at an `await`, and a resume
  shows it above whatever settled its promise (usually a callback like
  `advance`). Stepping over an `await` that suspends lands in the next code
  the runtime runs.
- **`--optimize` bakes are for shipping, not debugging.** The optimised
  Luau bake keeps line numbers but not the locals panel; the optimised
  AnimaScript bake carries no line probes at all, so its breakpoints stay
  hollow and nothing stops. A project with `dangerouslyFast: true` in its
  `rive.yaml` takes that optimized bake for AnimaScript too.
- **AnimaScript shows frames, not variables.** Breakpoints, stepping,
  the call stack and stops on traps work; locals and hover stay empty
  until a later bake can spill locals. The View Models scope still shows. A generator body is a frame
  under its own name for each `next()`.
- **Hover and Watch evaluate names, not expressions.** Dotted paths walk
  tables, vectors and Rive objects, so `self.size.x` works; `self.size.x * 2`
  does not.


## TOPIC: project/rive-yaml

# Projects and `rive.yaml`

A project is a directory containing a `rive.yaml`. Everything else in it is
bundled by file extension:

| Extension | Becomes |
|---|---|
| `.luau` | scripts — protocol scripts and importable modules |
| `.as` | AnimaScript, the same; needs `scripting: wasm` |
| `.wgsl` | shaders, compiled to RSTB |
| `.rml` | the scene, in as many files as you like, compiled as one document |
| `.png` `.jpg` `.jpeg` `.webp` | image assets |
| anything else | a blob asset, findable by name from scripts |

**The table is how sources are *discovered*, not a promise that everything in
the directory ends up in the `.riv`.** Assets are embedded when something
references them — a `file=` in the RML, or a `context:image` / blob lookup by
name from a script. A stray `notes.txt`, a font nothing uses, or the generator
script that wrote your scene adds nothing to the output, so `exclude` is for
keeping the *scan* tidy (and for keeping a second `.rml` from being picked up),
not for keeping weight out of the file.

**Every `.rml` in the tree is part of the scene.** A spare copy such as
`scene-old.rml` compiles alongside `scene.rml` and fails with duplicate ids.
Move it out, list it under `exclude`, or give it a leading dot.

Some files are never sources, and editing them doesn't trigger a rebuild in
`rive run`:

- anything whose name starts with `.` (a `.backup/` directory, `.scene-copy.rml`)
- `.riv`, `.rev` and `.log` files, and editor backups ending in `~`
- the output directory and the `logs` paths
- whatever `exclude` lists

Anything else the watcher sees counts as a source, so a tool that writes
inside the project (a `.txt` or `.json` log, say) rebuilds on every write.
Point it outside the project, at a `.log` name, or add it to `exclude`.

Only `name` is required:

```yaml
name: myproject
```

`rive create <dir>` writes a `rive.yaml` with `name` taken from the directory
and log paths under `build/`, plus a `scene.rml` holding an empty artboard,
timeline and state machine, `AGENTS.md`, a `CLAUDE.md` that imports it, and a
`.gitignore` for `build/`.
Existing files are left alone.

## Starting from an editor file

```bash
rive create demo --from-rev=demo_file.rev    # or omit demo: the .rev's name is used
rive demo
```

`--from-rev` converts an editor `.rev` into a project: `scene.rml` with every
script, shader and asset written as a file and referenced with `file=`, then
the usual scaffold. Files land where the Assets panel had them — the folder
tree in the editor becomes the directory tree on disk:

    Assets panel                demo/
