      main                        rive.yaml
      ui/                         scene.rml
        button                    main.luau
      images/                     ui/button.luau
        logo                      images/logo.png
      fonts/                      fonts/Inter.ttf
        Inter

Scripts keep working because a script's path *is* its module path: the editor's
`require('ui/button')` resolves to `ui/button.luau`. The directory must be empty
or new — the conversion writes a tree it cannot check file by file, so it never
merges into one.

The result is an ordinary project: `.luau` and `.wgsl` compile,
`png`/`jpg`/`jpeg`/`webp` are images, and fonts, svg, audio and other binaries
are blobs — still referenced correctly through `file=`, just not typed by the
scanner. Editor-only state (collaboration cursors, diff history) is dropped;
hosted fonts with no embedded bytes stay unresolved, as in any hand-written rml.

`--from-remote-file` runs the same conversion on a file in your Rive account
rather than a `.rev` on disk, and records it under `push:` so `rive push`
sends your edits back. With no value it lists your projects and files to pick
from; `--from-remote-file=<fileId>` goes straight to one. See
[push.md](../push.md).

## Full shape

```yaml
name: myproject
main: main
alwaysWatermark: true        # watermark every publish, whatever the plan; default false

artboard:
  width: 800
  height: 600
  background: "#1D1D1D"      # quote it -- a bare # starts a YAML comment

artboards:
  main:
    width: 1920
    height: 1080

exclude:
  - docs

excludeFromRev:
  scripts:
    - "*_test"
  artboards:
    - tests/*
  assets:
    - raw_*
  contents:
    - logo

libraries:                   # written by the tool, see Libraries below
  "palette":
    fileId: 4002
    libraryId: 42
    version: 1
    override: ../palette     # optional, and the only part you write

revFlavor: editable          # or "library"

push:
  projectId: 5336
  fileId: 24227

pages:
  teamId: 77
  name: "my-scene"

window:                      # icon on every desktop, see below; the rest is macOS only
  icon:                      # the process icon, or false for the stock one
    color: "#2b6b5e"         # behind the R; default black
    label: MT                # up to three characters; default the name's initials
    artboard: Icon           # or draw this artboard of the project instead
  titleBar: integrated       # or "standard" (default)
  controls:                  # traffic-light position, points from the top-left
    x: 16
    y: 19
  dragHeight: 52             # the strip a press drags the window from
  statusBar: false           # hide the stats strip (paid plans)
  hiddenFrameRate: 60        # advances a second while hidden; 0 pauses

cursor:
  property: cursor

app:                         # what rive build ships the project as
  id: com.example.myproject  # required for --package; default app.rive.<name>
  title: My Project          # under the icon; default the name
  version: "1.2.0"           # quote it; default 1.0.0
  icon: icon.png             # 1024x1024 PNG, no transparency; default the R
  allowNet: true             # scripts may fetch() https: URLs; default false
  aot: true                  # compile scripts ahead of time; default false
  orientation: portrait      # or landscape; default any
  statusBar: false           # hide the iOS status bar; default true
  team: ABCDE12345           # Apple team that signs; default the keychain's first

output:
  dir: build

logs:
  file: build/rive.log
  problems: build/problems.log
```

## Keys

**`name`** — required. Also the name other projects use to import this one.
A first `rive push` names the Rive file it creates after it; see
[push.md](../push.md#the-first-push).

**`main`** — which artboard is the file's default, by name. Without it, the
first artboard declared wins in an RML project, and the first layout script
alphabetically in a script-only one. A name that matches no artboard fails the
build.

**`scripting`** — `bytecode` (default) or `wasm`. `wasm` is required for
`.as` files; see [../animascript/protocols.md](../animascript/protocols.md).

**`wasmSimd`** — which WebAssembly SIMD the AnimaScript module may use: `on`
(default) for fixed-width SIMD, `off` for a scalar module that also runs in
browsers without wasm SIMD (Safari before 16.4), or `relaxed` to also fuse
multiply-adds, whose results can differ by platform; natively those need the
AOT lane, and browsers need relaxed SIMD support. A script that uses no SIMD
bakes the same either way. The job, worker and audio processor modules bake
with the same setting as the main module. A browser that lacks the SIMD a file
was baked with runs none of the file's scripts, lanes included, and says so on
the console: `this browser lacks WebAssembly SIMD, so this file's scripts are
off; bake with wasmSimd: off to support it`. The editor keeps the same setting
on the file's Backboard.

**`wasmMaxPages`** — the most memory the AnimaScript module can grow to, in
pages of 64 KB, so 4096 is 256 MB. The module starts with what its static data
needs and grows as it allocates. When it needs more than the cap allows, it
traps and the log says it hit its wasmMaxPages ceiling. A bake fails if its
static data alone needs more. Left out, the module can grow to 4 GB, all that
wasm32 can address, or until the device runs out of memory. A file with
parallel calls grows the same way, between calls. Each thread its calls run
on besides the main lane's takes 64 KB of it, made at its first call. Near
the cap there may be no room for that, and the calls then run on fewer
threads; see [../animascript/threading.md](../animascript/threading.md).

**`audioBuffer`** — the buffer of the watch window's audio device, in frames
from 16 to 8192. Left out, the device opens with its default of about 10 ms. A
bigger buffer keeps a heavy audio processor from dropping out on a loaded
machine, at the cost of that much more latency. `--audio-buffer=<frames>`
overrides it for one run. The device opens once, when the window does, so an
edit applies the next time `rive <dir>` starts. The buffer is fitted to the
output the window opened on, so after switching outputs, restart to fit the new
one. A device can round or clamp the size; the log then says what buffer it
opened with. Headless runs open no device and ignore the key.

**`debugLevel`**, **`optimizationLevel`** — the editor's publish levels for
scripts, `none`, `medium` or `max`; defaults `none` and `max`.

**`shaderOutputs`** — the shader backends compiled on publish, a list from
`msl`, `glsl`, `wgsl`, `hlsl`, `spirv`; default all of them. These three and
`main` are what the editor keeps on the file's Backboard, which a fragment
never declares; `create --from-rev` writes them here from a rev.

**`wasmFuel`** — `true` meters the release AnimaScript module (`--optimize`,
`--bench`, `rive build` and publishes) with fuel, so every runtime stops a
runaway script at its time budget, browsers included. Its job, worker and
audio processor modules carry fuel too, so a browser can also end a stopped
job or worker that never polls, a lane holding the page's thread past the
time budget, and a processor block past its hard limit; see
[../animascript/threading.md](../animascript/threading.md). Natively the host
interrupts lanes with fuel or without, so there their fuel only costs speed.
Off by default: a release module then asks native runtimes for their watchdog
and runs unbounded in browsers, which have none, and there a stopped job or
worker ends only where it polls or awaits. Fuel costs a few percent in loops
on V8 and WAMR AOT, 20 to 60% on the WAMR interpreter, and most in deep
recursion, where a recursive `fib` runs about 2.4x slower on V8 and 2.5 to
2.8x on WAMR AOT. In an audio processor it makes each block about a fifth to a
third slower, and in a browser up to nearly twice as slow when its loops do
very little each pass. Debug bakes, which the live window plays, always carry
fuel, in their lanes as well. The editor keeps the same setting on the file's
Backboard.

**`dangerouslyFast`** — `true` compiles the time budget out of every bake, the
live window's included, for trusted content whose long running builders the
budget would stop; a runaway script then hangs any host. It cannot be combined
with `wasmFuel`, and the editor refuses to run a module baked with it.

**`alwaysWatermark`** — `true` puts the watermark, the Rive splash screen, in
every `--publish`, `--publish=web` and `rive build` app of a project with
`.rml` markup, even when the account would publish clean. Publishing still
needs a signed-in account. Off by default, which leaves it to the account. A
script-only project publishes without a watermark either way. The live window stays clean either
way. The editor keeps the same setting on the file's Backboard as "Always show
splash screen", and `create --from-rev` and `rive pull` write it here from a
rev.

**`artboard`** — default size and background for generated artboards. Applies
only when there is no `.rml`; RML artboards carry their own dimensions.
`background` must be quoted.

**`artboards`** — per-artboard overrides, keyed by name.

**`exclude`** — paths not to bundle at all.

**`excludeFromRev`** — drops matching things from the exported `.rev` only. The
`.riv` and the live window always contain everything. Four categories:

- `scripts` — by module path, Luau and WGSL
- `artboards` — by name
- `assets` — by name
- `contents` — asset *bytes*, keeping the asset referenced but unembedded

Patterns support `*` (any run of characters, including `/`) and `?` (one
character). Excluding a layout script also drops its generated artboard.

**`libraries`** — the libraries published in Rive that this project's scene
imports directly. The tool writes it; `override` on an entry is the one part
that is yours. See [Libraries](#libraries) below.

**`revFlavor`** — `editable` (default) or `library`. Controls whether the
exported `.rev` opens as a normal editor file or as a library others import.

**`push`** — the Rive file `rive push` updates. Written back automatically by
the first push (`projectId` picks where the file is created, `fileId` binds
later pushes to it), and by `rive create --from-remote-file`, which binds the
project to the file it was made from; edit or remove it to retarget.

**`pages`** — the hosted page `rive <dir> --publish=web` replaces. Written
back by the first publish and not touched after: `teamId` is the team that
owns the page, `name` the slug it answers to. Edit `name` to publish to a
different page; remove the block to be asked again. See
[publish-web.md](../publish-web.md).

**`window`** — how the live window frames the scene. `icon` reaches every
desktop; the rest is macOS only, and every other desktop keeps its ordinary
frame. `--screenshot` and the other headless runs never open a
window and ignore the block entirely.

- `icon` — the process icon while the project is open, in the Dock and
  Cmd-Tab on macOS and the taskbar and window switcher on Windows and
  Linux, so several previews tell apart. By default the R carries the
  project name's initials in a badge: the first letter of the first two
  words, or the first two letters of a single word. `label` sets up to three
  characters of `A-Z` and `0-9` instead and `color` a hex colour behind the
  R. `icon: false` keeps the stock icon. `artboard` names an artboard of the
  project to draw as the icon instead, clipped to the icon shape and redrawn
  on every build, with its default state machine and view model instance
  advanced once. The window title leads with the name either way; the
  Dock's hover label and the Cmd-Tab caption are the executable's file
  name, which macOS never lets a process change. On Wayland only
  compositors with `xdg-toplevel-icon` show the icon; the rest keep the app
  id's.
- `titleBar` — macOS only. `standard` (default) keeps the usual title bar
  strip above the scene. `integrated` draws the scene across the whole
  window, under the native close, minimize and zoom controls, with no strip
  of its own: the artboard is laid out to the full window height and the
  title text is hidden. The controls stay native, so their hover,
  accessibility and full-screen behaviour is the system's. Edits to the
  block apply to the running window on the next build, like any other edit.
  These settings apply to standalone preview windows. On macOS, `rive editor`
  always uses its own integrated header (controls at `16, 18`, drag height
  `52`), including detached pane windows; the preview stays inside its pane.
- `controls` — where the native controls sit, `x` and `y` in points from the
  window's top-left corner. Only read with `titleBar: integrated`; leave the
  block out for the stock placement. A `y` deeper than the stock strip grows
  the strip, so a 52pt header centres its controls with `y: 19`.
- `dragHeight` — the strip along the top, in points, where a press on nothing
  interactive drags the window. A listener target, a text input or a scripted
  layout with pointer handlers keeps its presses. Left out, the strip is the
  height of the native controls; zero turns dragging off.
- `statusBar` — the 28 point strip along the bottom of the preview window
  with frame times, script heap, process memory, the script VM and who is
  signed in. The scene is laid out above it, so it never covers content.
  `false` hides it on a paid plan; free and signed out accounts always see
  it. `--no-status-bar` and the `b` terminal command do the same. It is
  never drawn in screenshots, `--bench` or other headless runs.
- `hiddenFrameRate` — how many times a second the scene advances while the
  window can't draw: fully covered, minimised, hidden, on another Space, or
  mid-switch to another app. Nothing is drawn then and the process sleeps
  between advances, but the scene keeps its timing, so state machines,
  timers and scripts that schedule audio from `advance` carry on, and the
  time between advances is never lost. Defaults to `60`; lower it to save
  power, raise it for a scene that schedules only a short way ahead. `0`
  pauses the scene while the window can't be seen and resumes it where it
  left off once it can. A script's audio processor runs on its own thread,
  so sound it is already making carries on; only `advance` stops.

The scene learns where the chrome is through two numbers written into the
artboard's bound view model instance when it declares them: `titleBarHeight`
and `titleBarControlsWidth`, in points, both zero in full screen. Bind a
header's height and a spacer's width to them. The
[integrated_titlebar](../../samples/integrated_titlebar) sample is the
worked example: `rive "$(rive samples --path)/integrated_titlebar"`.

**`cursor.property`** — opt in to native cursors: the string or enum
property (a path on the artboard's bound view model, as `--data` spells one)
the scene writes cursor names into. The previewer shows what it names; without the key the OS cursor is never touched. See
[../cursor.md](../cursor.md).

**`app`** — what `rive build` ships the project as in our player. Flags win
over each key, and nothing here changes the live window. The block rides the
file's Backboard, so a push carries it to the Rive file and a pull or
`rive create` from that file brings it back. A file that never carried one
leaves the local block alone.

- `id` — the bundle id or package name. App Store Connect knows the app by
  it, so `--package` requires it and it should not change once the app
  exists there. Without it a device build makes up `app.rive.<name>`, with
  your signing team appended on iOS.
- `title` — the name under the icon; `--title` wins over it.
- `version` — the version people see, up to three numbers.
- `icon` — the iOS app icon, relative to the project: a 1024x1024 PNG with
  no transparency, which App Store Connect requires.
- `allowNet` — the app's scripts may `fetch()` https: URLs, as `--allow-net`
  lets them on the host. Only iOS has a transport so far.
- `aot` — compile the scripts into the app ahead of time, as `--aot` does.
- `orientation` — `portrait` or `landscape` locks the app, which on iPad
  also opts out of multitasking; `any` (default) turns with the device.
- `statusBar` — `false` hides the iOS status bar.
- `team` — the Apple team id that signs iOS builds, ten characters as
  `security find-identity -v -p codesigning` shows it; default the first
  identity in the keychain.

See [Store builds](../../README.md#store-builds).

**The `ios/` folder** — anything else an iOS app needs, beside `rive.yaml`.
`rive build` lays it over our player's own iOS files, so what it holds
replaces or joins theirs:

- Sources (`.m`, `.mm`, `.swift`, `.cpp`) compile into the app target, Swift
  as 5.0. Module imports link their frameworks, so `@import GameKit;` or
  `import GameKit` is all Game Center needs.
- `App.entitlements` is the app's entitlements file, such as
  `com.apple.developer.game-center`. Automatic signing adds its capabilities
  to the app id and profile, which takes an Apple account in Xcode or the
  `EVI_ASC_KEY_*` App Store Connect key. With `--hardware-bounds`, rive build
  adds `com.apple.developer.kernel.extended-virtual-addressing` to it: without
  it an app on a current iPhone has too little address space for hardware
  bounds checks.
- `Assets.xcassets` and `PrivacyInfo.xcprivacy` replace the player's. The
  `app.icon` key still replaces any app icon in the catalog.
- `Info.plist` is merged, not copied. The keys `app` stands for win, then
  this file's, then the player's, then the ones evi generates.

Every other file in the folder goes into the app too.

**`output.dir`** — where the `.riv` is written. Defaults to `build`.

**`logs.file`** — append-only interleave of compiler problems, script `print`
output and system messages.

**`logs.problems`** — rewritten atomically per build with a generation header,
so it always reflects exactly one build. This is the file to read when
scripting around the tool.

## Libraries

A library is content published in the Rive editor that other files import:
artboards, state machines, view models, enums, scripts and shaders. A project
made from a file that imports one arrives with everything it needs, and
`rive pull` keeps it current.

### The `libraries` block

```yaml
libraries:
  "palette":
    fileId: 4002
    libraryId: 42
    version: 1
```

Only the libraries this project's scene imports **directly**. A library that
another library imports is not listed: it arrives through that library, and
the project never names it.

The block mirrors what the remote file currently depends on. `rive create
--from-remote-file` writes it, and every `rive pull` rewrites it: entries
appear as the file gains dependencies and disappear as it loses them, and
`version` follows the newest version the file reaches for.

**Do not hand-edit the three fields.** `fileId`, `libraryId` and `version` are
the tool's, and the next pull overwrites whatever is there. `scriptMode` is
yours to set, though a pull also writes the file's value into it. Comments
and any other key inside an entry survive a rewrite untouched.

The key is the library's name, lowercased with anything outside
`[a-z0-9_-.]` replaced by `_`, quoted so a library called `123` stays a name
rather than becoming a number. It is also the label a `require` writes after
`lib:`:

```luau
local ink = require('lib:palette/ink')
```

Two libraries whose names reduce to the same key get `#` and the library id
appended to tell them apart, as in `"face_mesh#42"`. The require label follows
the key.

Changing which libraries a file imports, or which version it uses, is editor
work today. A later CLI will do it from here: updating a dependency to a newer
published version, adding one, and publishing a new version of a project whose
own file is a library.

### The `.libraries` folder

A project that imports libraries holds a `.libraries/` folder beside its
markup. `create --from-remote-file` and `pull` download into it every library
the file reaches, directly and indirectly, and the build reads it to assemble
the `.riv` (or the `.rev` with `--rev`). Nothing at play time looks at it: by
then the library content is inside the file.

It is committed with the project rather than ignored, so a teammate who clones
can build without pulling, and without needing access to the libraries
themselves.

**Treat it as read-only.** Edits inside it are picked up by a running build,
which makes it tempting, but they are lost the moment that content is fetched
again, with nothing reporting it. The folder is derived and disposable:
deleting it costs one `rive pull`. Its contents are described in
[libraries-folder.md](libraries-folder.md) as background, not as something to
maintain.

### Libraries the editor bundles

The editor's TextInput component does not come from a library published in
Rive. The editor ships that library inside itself and marks what it places
with reserved ids: `libraryId="592"` and `assetId="1"`, with no
`libraryVersionId`. The backend has no snapshot by that id, so there is
nothing for `rive pull` to download.

The CLI carries the same markup the editor instances and resolves those
assets from it. Such a library never appears in `.libraries/` or the lock,
and needs no `libraries` entry in `rive.yaml`. A folder under `.libraries/`
named for the same snapshot, `@1`, still wins, for checking a change to the
component before the editor ships it.

### Working on a library locally

An `override` points the build at a local rive-cli project instead of the
snapshots `rive pull` downloaded into `.libraries/`, so a library and a file
that imports it can be edited together without publishing between every
change:

```yaml
libraries:
  "palette":
    fileId: 4002
    libraryId: 42
    version: 1
    # resolve from the project next door while I work on it
    override: ../palette
```

It is yours, unlike the three fields above it. A pull rewrites those and
leaves this and any comment beside it alone.

The override has to be a rive-cli project whose own `push.fileId` is the
library's `fileId`, which is what stops a path typo resolving against some
unrelated project. If it is not, the build says so and falls back to those
snapshots:

```
warning  rive.yaml:1:1  [lint] for library palette, the override ../palette
pushes to file 7701, not the library's 4002; falling back to the downloaded
library in .libraries/
```

The same line, with a different reason in the middle, covers a path that is
not a project, a `rive.yaml` that cannot be read, and a project holding no
markup.

**An override changes what the build resolves, never the markup.** The scene
still names the library and the version it always did, and the file you push
is unchanged by it. The project builds as before the moment you remove the
key.

A component the override no longer carries falls back to the downloaded
snapshot, so a half-finished local copy still builds. Each build says what it
got:

```
library override ../palette provides all 3 components the host needs from
the library
```

and says `provides none of the 3` when the fileId check refused it, which is
the quickest way to notice that the warning above scrolled past.

The override's own libraries are not overridden in turn: a library you edit
locally still imports its own dependencies from `.libraries/`.

Editing a file under the override triggers a rebuild, the same as editing the
project's own sources.

### How a library's scripts compile

A library's AnimaScript compiles differently from your own in a preview
build, and `scriptMode` chooses how:

```yaml
libraries:
  "draco":
    fileId: 4100
    libraryId: 51
    version: 3
    scriptMode: fast
```

| `scriptMode` | Debugger | Runaway loops |
|---|---|---|
| `bounded`, the default | never enters it | stopped on desktop by the watchdog, on the web by fuel checks |
| `fast` | never enters it | stopped on desktop by the watchdog; nothing stops them on the web |
| `debug` | breakpoints and stepping, like your own code | fuel checks everywhere, like your own code |

`bounded` and `fast` leave out the debugger probes, which are what slow a
heavy library most in a preview, so its code runs much faster than your own.
`fast` matters for the web, where only the fuel checks can stop a runaway loop
and they slow every loop the library runs.

A library's code in a job, worker or audio processor compiles by its mode too,
just as on the main lane, except that the debugger never steps into those
lanes.

`fast` is part of the file, so it applies to everyone who opens it, on the web
too.

The mode is part of the file, so the editor's inspector for the library shows
the same value: a pull writes it here and a build or push writes it back. An
override is always compiled as `debug`, since you are working on it, without
changing what the file says. Release builds ignore the mode.

### What the build tells you

A library the project does not hold is a warning, not an error. The file
builds without what that library supplies, which is the same partial state the
editor shows, and a `rive pull` that reaches the library fixes it.

A project that imports **two versions of one library** can lose a script or a
shader that the newer version did not republish. The build says so, naming the
snapshot and both versions. There is no way to avoid it from the project
side: import a single version where you can, or have the library republish
that script in the newer version.

### Pushing

`rive push` sends the project's own content. A library's artboards and scripts
stay out of the `.rev` it writes, because they belong to the library's file
rather than to this one.

## Layout on disk

Nothing is enforced beyond `rive.yaml` being at the root. A conventional
project:

```
myproject/
  rive.yaml
  scene.rml
  main.luau
  mathutil.luau
  mathutil_test.luau
  Montserrat.ttf
  logo.png
  build/
```

A project that imports published libraries has one more, holding what `rive
pull` downloaded:

```
myproject/
  rive.yaml
  scene.rml
  .libraries/
```

What is inside it is the tool's, and
[libraries-folder.md](libraries-folder.md) describes it for anyone who wants
to know. Nothing in a project should depend on that shape.

Asset paths in RML are project-relative:

```xml
<FontAsset file="Montserrat.ttf" name="Montserrat" id="0:30"/>
<ScriptAsset file="main.luau" name="main" id="0:80"/>
```

## Commands

```bash
rive create <dir>                 # scaffold yaml, scene.rml, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md, .gitignore
rive create <dir> --from-rev=f.rev  # the same, but scene.rml and its files come from an editor .rev
rive create <dir> --from-remote-file[=<fileId>]  # the same, from a file in your Rive account
rive <dir> --verify               # build once, exit non-zero on errors
rive <dir> --test                 # build, run every Tests script, exit non-zero on failures
rive <dir> --rev=out.rev          # export an editor .rev
rive inspect <dir> --json         # dump the built scene and any ignored input
rive <dir> --artboard=<name>      # choose the artboard shown on launch
rive <dir> --optimize             # compile scripts at Luau O2 instead of O1, and AnimaScript without debugger line probes (several times faster, for timing and long tests)
rive <dir> --release              # a release build of the scripts, as a publish ships them: asserts and the checks inside unchecked code compiled out; the status bar says RELEASE, OPTIMIZED with --optimize, DEBUG otherwise
```

A directory literally named `create` or `login` must be passed as `./create`
or `./login`, so it is not read as the subcommand.

In macOS **editor mode**, the workspace always uses an integrated title bar,
with controls at `(16, 18)` and a 52-point drag strip. Project `window.titleBar`,
`controls`, and `dragHeight` settings apply to standalone previews; they do not
change the editor workspace header. Detached editor windows use the same header.

**RML editor formatting** — controls the built-in editor's format action (F4)
and format-on-save (Cmd+S on macOS):

```yaml
editor:
  rml:
    indentSize: 2
    printWidth: 80
    multilineAttributes: auto
```

- `indentSize`: positive integer spaces per nesting level (default `4`). Also controls
  RML indent guides, Tab, Shift+Tab, and automatic indentation.
- `printWidth`: positive integer character target (default `80`). Includes the
  opening tag's indentation, attributes, spaces, and closing `>` or `/>`.
  When explicitly set, a faint vertical guide marks that column in RML code
  panes and follows horizontal scrolling. Omitting it hides the guide while
  retaining the default formatting target.
- `multilineAttributes`: `false` (default) keeps attributes inline; `true`
  always puts each attribute on its own line; `auto` does so only when the
  complete opening tag would exceed `printWidth`. Tags exactly at the limit
  remain inline. Previously wrapped tags collapse again when they fit.

With `auto`, a short tag stays inline:

```xml
<Shape name="Background" />
```

A tag exceeding the target places each property on its own line, one indent
level deeper, and aligns the closing bracket with the opening tag:

```xml
<Shape
  name="Background"
  x="12"
  y="24"
/>
```

`printWidth` is a formatting target, not a hard limit or visual word-wrap:
individual values, comments, and text are never split. UTF-8 characters count
as one character each. Attribute values containing literal newlines use
multiline layout in `auto` mode.

Save `rive.yaml` first; formatting reads these preferences without a restart.
Indent guides also refresh when the project rebuilds. Formatting normalizes
existing element indentation in element-only content. It preserves attribute
order, quote styles, entity spellings, comments, CDATA, mixed text, and
whitespace in `xml:space="preserve"` content. It does not add line breaks between
inline elements. Malformed XML and unsupported declarations (such as DOCTYPE)
are left untouched, with a Console message. These settings apply to RML in the
built-in editor; other languages and external LSP clients retain their existing
formatting behavior.

## Personal code editor settings

Appearance and typography are configured per user in `$RIVE_HOME/settings.yaml`, defaulting to
`~/.rive/settings.yaml` (using `USERPROFILE` on Windows when `HOME` is unset).
When signed in, click your titlebar avatar and choose **Editor settings** to open
Settings on any platform. The same menu includes **Account settings**, which opens
your account page in the browser, and **Sign out**.
On macOS, you can also choose **Rive → Settings…** (`⌘,`); on Windows and Linux, press
**Ctrl+,**. This opens the file in Hydrogen, creating its directory and commented
defaults if needed. It applies across CLI editor projects;
these preferences are not stored in `rive.yaml` or sent by `rive push`.

```yaml
editor:
  theme: dark # light or dark
  code:
    fontSize: 16
    lineHeight: 24
    font:
      path: fonts/MyMono.ttf
```

`fontSize` accepts numbers from 6 to 96, and `lineHeight` from 6 to 192.
Both are logical pixels; line height is an absolute height, not a multiplier.
Omitted values use the defaults shown above. Omit `font`, or use an empty
`path`, to use the embedded font. Custom TTF and OTF files use a single face
for all syntax scopes. Installed family names and weight selection are not
yet supported.

Font paths may be absolute or relative to the directory containing
`settings.yaml`. Home-directory (`~`) and environment-variable expansion are
not performed. Keeping personal fonts alongside this settings file keeps them
out of project asset collection.

The running editor checks settings and the selected font file approximately
once per second. Changes apply to open and newly opened text panes, including
detached panes. Invalid settings keep the last valid preferences and report a
Console message. An unreadable or invalid font falls back to the embedded font
with a Console message. Deleting the settings file restores defaults.

`editor.theme` accepts `light` or `dark` (default). Saving a change updates the entire
editor, including detached panes. The titlebar appearance button writes the
same setting, replacing the old per-layout `.theme` preference. With an open,
unsaved settings tab, the button changes that buffer and previews the theme;
save the tab to persist it. It never silently saves unrelated edits.
The button preserves comments in ordinary block YAML. Unusual flow mappings
or quoted theme keys may be reserialized while retaining their setting values.

### Console typography

The Console inherits each omitted typography field from `editor.code`.
Override any of the same fields independently:

```yaml
editor:
  console:
    fontSize: 14
    lineHeight: 20
    font:
      path: fonts/MyConsoleFont.ttf
```

The same numeric limits and path resolution rules apply. Removing an override
restores inheritance; an explicit `font.path: ""` selects the embedded font
instead of inheriting a custom code font. Missing or invalid font files fall
back to the embedded font with a Console message. Changes apply to existing
log rows without clearing output, retaining tail-following or the visible row
when scrolled back. Console settings do not change the Problems pane.


## TOPIC: project/libraries-folder

# Inside `.libraries`

> **Nothing here is yours to edit, and nothing should be built on it.**
>
> `.libraries/` is working storage the tool writes and rewrites. An edit
> inside it is picked up by a running build, which makes it look like a place
> to work, and is then lost the moment that content is downloaded again, with
> nothing reporting it. Delete the folder and a `rive pull` rebuilds it.
>
> This page describes the shape as of `lockVersion: 1`, for anyone who wants
> to know what a `rive pull` left behind. It is not an interface. Expect it to
> change, and do not write anything that reads it.

What a project does with libraries, and the `libraries:` block that names
them, is in [rive-yaml.md](rive-yaml.md).

## The shape

```
myproject/
  rive.yaml
  scene.rml
  .libraries/
    lock.yaml
    bonhomme_eye@118810/
    bonhomme_eye@118811/
    bonhomme_head_and_hat@118813/
```

One folder per **snapshot**, plus a lock file. A snapshot is the content one
publish of a library produced, converted to markup. The folder is named for
the library and the backend's id for that snapshot, after the `@`.

A library appears more than once when the project reaches more than one of
its publishes, which is why `bonhomme_eye` is here twice.

## A snapshot folder

```
bonhomme_head_and_hat@118813/
  rive.yaml
  scene.rml
  faceimage.png
```

It looks like a rive-cli project and is not one. The `rive.yaml` holds a name
and the main artboard, and nothing reads it: the build finds the markup by
scanning for `.rml` and identifies the snapshot by the folder name. It is
there so someone opening the folder can see what they are looking at.

**Do not run `rive` on one.** A snapshot that imports another library names it
the way any document does, and the content it names lives in the **host's**
`.libraries`, not inside the snapshot. So the snapshot alone cannot resolve
its own imports:

```xml
<!-- in bonhomme_head_and_hat@118813/scene.rml -->
<LibraryAsset libraryId="623" libraryVersionId="1645" assetId="118810" name="bonhomme_eye"/>
```

`bonhomme_eye@118810` is a sibling of that folder, not a child. Only the
project at the root holds the whole graph.

## `lock.yaml`

Everything a snapshot cannot say about itself. The snapshot's bytes never
mention which library or version they belong to, and the folder name carries
only the snapshot id, so the lock is what joins them up.

```yaml
# Generated by Rive CLI. Do not edit
lockVersion: 1
revToRmlVersion: 1

libraries:
  bonhomme_eye:
    libraryId: 623
    fileId: 37316
    versions:
      1:
        libraryVersionId: 1645
        components:
          - { coreId: "0-2", type: artboard, name: "Eye", folder: bonhomme_eye@118810 }
      2:
        libraryVersionId: 1646
        description: "Black iris"
        components:
          - { coreId: "0-2", type: artboard, name: "Eye", folder: bonhomme_eye@118811 }

folders:
  bonhomme_eye@118810:
    library: bonhomme_eye
    assetId: 118810
    imports: []
  bonhomme_head_and_hat@118813:
    library: bonhomme_head_and_hat
    assetId: 118813
    imports:
      - bonhomme_eye@118810
```

**`lockVersion`** — how this file is spelled. A build that reads a different
one refuses the project rather than guessing, because reading it with the
wrong rules would answer the published-component check on nonsense. Deleting
`.libraries` and pulling again is the remedy.

**`revToRmlVersion`** — which build's conversion the folders are. A snapshot is
the markup this build makes of those bytes, not the bytes, so a build whose
conversion differs downloads them again.

**`libraries`** — what each published version holds. The key is the library's
name as the project spells it, matching the `libraries:` block in `rive.yaml`.
Each version lists its components by their core id, type and name, and for
each one, the folder carrying it.

That last field is the point of the section. **A version spans as many
snapshots as it has publishes behind it**: a publish that touches one
component leaves every other pointing at the snapshot of the publish that last
touched it. So a component's folder is per component, not per version.

**`folders`** — one row per snapshot on disk: which library owns it, its
snapshot id, and the snapshots its own markup imports. The `imports` list lets
a pull walk the graph without reading markup.

## What a pull does with it

A snapshot's id names bytes that can never change, because a publish writes
that id once and the asset store keys content by its own digest. So a folder
an earlier pull wrote for that id is still correct, and a later pull keeps it
rather than downloading it again.

What that does not cover is the conversion, which is what `revToRmlVersion` is
for, and the shape of the lock itself, which is what `lockVersion` is for. A
mismatch in either throws the folders away.

A pull that cannot reach some library writes what it did reach and reports the
rest. It never deletes a folder it merely failed to hear about.


## TOPIC: publishing

# Building and publishing

| Mode | Produces | Needs a login |
|---|---|---|
| `--verify` | nothing; compiles and reports | no |
| *(no flag)* — live window, watches for edits | a preview; the build stays in memory | no |
| `--publish` | a **signed** `.riv` on disk | **yes** |
| `--publish=local` | the explicit synonym of the bare form above | **yes** |
| `--publish=web` | a hosted page: build, sign, upload | **yes** |
| `--unpublish=web` | takes a hosted page down | **yes** |
| `--list-published` | where this project is published, local and web | no\* |
| `--test` | runs the `Tests` scripts | no |
| `--screenshot` | a png of one frame, rendered headless | no |

\* `--list-published` reads the API only if the project already has a
`pages:` binding — an unpublished project answers entirely from disk and
exits 0. When the project does have a `pages:` binding, a failure to read the
web row causes `--list-published` to exit non-zero and print the reason to stderr.
`--list-published=web` always needs a session: it asks for the team's live
pages, not this project's.

The build modes are mutually exclusive — pick one. Running with no flag is the
default: it opens the live window and rebuilds as you edit.

Only handing the work on needs a session: `--publish` to ship it, `--rev` and
`rive push` to pass it to the editor. The session is checked live, so those
fail offline even with stored credentials.

## Which one you want

**`--verify` while authoring.** Full local compile — RML, Luau, WGSL — writing
nothing. It is the fastest loop, so it is what to run after every edit. See
[luau/protocols.md](luau/protocols.md#checking-a-script).

**`--publish` for a `.riv` file.** It writes the signed `.riv` to disk, as do
`--publish=web` and `rive build` on their way to a page or an app. The
scripts are compiled server-side and signed, and the account decides the
watermark unless `rive.yaml` sets `alwaysWatermark: true`. `--verify`,
`--test`, `--screenshot` and the live window keep the build in memory. A
publish the plan watermarks says so, with where to upgrade:

```
watermarked: the Rive splash screen plays on Free. Publish without it on any paid plan: https://rive.app/pricing
```

### Signing in

`--publish` and `--rev` require a signed-in session:

```bash
rive login
```

That prints a URL and a short code. Approve it in a browser on any device and
the CLI picks the session up, and the session persists — you do it once, not
per build. On a desktop it opens the page for you; over SSH, on a remote box or
under an agent, open the URL wherever you have a browser. Check that the page
shows the same code as your terminal before you approve.

`rive whoami` shows who you are signed in as, `rive logout` clears it.

Signing is a separate matter from the session. Watch builds **unsigned**, and the live window plays unsigned scripts without complaint —
so watching a file tells you nothing about whether it is shippable. Only
`--publish` signs.

Without it, `--publish` stops before sending anything and writes no file.
Somewhere no one can sign in at all — CI, a container — every other mode still
works, so you can author, build, test and capture.
Handing the work on, with `--publish` or `--rev`, has to run somewhere signed
in.

Credentials live outside the project — `~/.config/rive/app.rive.cli/` on
macOS and Linux, Credential Manager on Windows. A process with a different
`HOME` or user reports `Not logged in` even on a machine where you *are*
signed in, which is the usual reason an automated run fails when the same
command works in your own shell.

## Why signing exists

**A `.riv` whose scripts are unsigned is rejected by the CDN and the web
runtimes.** Nothing local tells you this: the CLI's own viewer builds with
tooling enabled and plays unsigned files happily, so a project can look
finished, run correctly in front of you, and fail the moment it is served.

If a file contains scripts and is destined for the web, it has to be built with
`--publish`. If it has no scripts, the distinction does not arise.

## What `--publish` does

1. Compiles locally first — syntax errors and WGSL problems still stop the
   build before anything is sent.
2. POSTs the rewritten Luau and WGSL to Rive's compile service and polls for
   the result.
3. Writes the returned bytecode plus a 64-byte aggregate signature into the
   built file.

It writes `build/<name>.riv`, or the folder `--output-dir` names.

**It fails closed.** Auth failure, network failure, or a timeout means no file
is written — you never get a silently-unsigned build from a publish that went
wrong.

The signing service has two hard caps, and the publish fails with its error
when a project goes over either:

| Limit | |
|---|---|
| 1000 scripts | more is an error, not a truncation |
| 10 MB request | the compiled payload total |

A project with **zero** scripts skips the service entirely and writes an
unsigned `.riv`, which is correct — there is nothing to sign.

## Exporting for the editor

`--rev=<path>` writes a `.rev`, on its own or alongside `--publish`:

```bash
rive myproject --rev=myproject.rev
```

The `.rev` is always unsigned source — it is the editable document, not a
runtime artifact — so signing has no bearing on it. It does need a session,
though: a `.rev` is the handoff into the editor, the same artifact
`rive push` delivers, so exporting one requires `rive login`. The window's
**File ▸ Export .rev…** is the same thing by another route and asks for the
same session.

`--rev` does not combine with
`--verify`, which by design writes nothing, nor with `--test`,
`--screenshot` or `--semantics`, which exit before the export.

Before handing a multi-artboard file to the editor, give each artboard an `x`
and `y`: that is its stage position, and artboards without one all land on
the origin. See [format.md](format.md#document-structure).

## Pushing to a Rive file

`rive push` skips the on-disk `.rev` entirely: it builds and sends the document
straight to a Rive file in your workspace, so the project opens from the
editor's file browser with a revision history.

```bash
rive login                        # once: same session as --publish
rive push                         # first push: creates the file, later
                                  # pushes update it
```

The first push creates the file (picking or prompting for a project) and
records it under `push:` in `rive.yaml`; every later push replaces its content
and adds a named entry to the revision history. [push.md](push.md) has the
full story.

`push`/`pull` move the *source document* between the CLI and the Rive editor,
for round-trip authoring with revision history; publishing ships the *built
artifact* to consumers. Different destinations, different things travel.

## Publishing to the web

```bash
rive myproject --publish=web      # build, sign, and host it at a url
```

Same signed build as `--publish`, uploaded to a page anyone can open — no
account needed to view it. Unlike `--rev` and `rive push`, which hand over the
editable document, this ships the built artifact: a url that plays, not a
project that opens.

The page belongs to a team, and its name identifies it: publishing that name
again replaces what the url serves. `--list-published=web` shows every live
page on the team, and `--unpublish=web` takes one down.
[publish-web.md](publish-web.md) has the full story.

## Scripting the one-shots

Exit codes are typed, so a pipeline can branch without parsing stderr:

| Code | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 0 | ok |
| 1 | build errors, or any failure without a more specific code |
| 2 | bad command line |
| 3 | not logged in, or the session was rejected |
| 6 | test cases failed (the build itself was fine) |
| 7 | a service could not be reached — safe to retry |
| 8 | this CLI is below the published minimum — run `rive update` |
| 9 | the monthly CLI allowance is used up; upgrade, top up or wait for the reset |

Except when an outdated CLI exits 8 before command dispatch, `--format=json`
on `--verify`, `--publish` or `--test` prints one JSON envelope
on stdout (`{"success", "command", "data", "errors", "warnings",
"allowance", "credits"}`) with the problem list (script, line, message) or
the test results (counts plus each failure's group path) under `data`. Lines
and columns are 1-based. Logs stay on stderr, so stdout is only the envelope.
`allowance` is `null` unless the run hit the monthly allowance, and `credits`
is `null` unless the run used credits; see below.

Without `--format=json`, `--publish` prints the file it wrote on stdout, so
the path can be taken the way `--publish=web` hands back a url:

```bash
path=$(rive myproject --publish --quiet | tail -1)
```

It prints nothing there when nothing was written — an output directory that
cannot be written to, say. The build itself still succeeded, so the exit code
is 0 and the reason is on stderr, which `--quiet` silences: test the path
rather than the status.

```bash
[ -n "$path" ] || { echo "nothing was published" >&2; exit 1; }
```

Publishing (`--publish`, `--publish=local`, `--publish=web`) and `rive build`
need edit access to the file in `push.fileId`. A Viewer gets "You need edit
access to this file to publish it from the CLI. Ask an admin of <Workspace>
for edit access." on stderr, even with `--quiet`, and exit 1. With
`--format=json` the line is in `errors`.

### The monthly allowance

Some plans cap how many pushes and publishes the CLI makes a month. On Free
it's 50, pushes and publishes together. The Workspace that owns the file
counts them; a project with no `push.fileId` counts against your personal
Workspace.

- A push counts when it completes. Before sending anything, `rive push` checks
  that the Workspace has one left.
- A publish counts when it starts, before signing, so a publish whose signing
  fails later still counts. A signed `.riv` for local testing
  (`--publish=local`) counts like any other publish.
- `--publish=web` counts once, as a publish.
- App builds (`rive build`) never count. Neither do pulls, or previewing
  locally with `--serve` or the live window.

Once the cap is reached, the next push or publish is refused with nothing
sent, and the CLI prints the reason with an upgrade link (a top-up link when
credits ran out, see below) and exits 9:

```
Monthly CLI allowance used up: 50 of 50 publishes and pushes. Resets Dec 1, 2026 (UTC). Upgrade: https://rive.app/pricing
```

It never retries that refusal. With `--format=json` the line is in `errors`,
and `allowance` holds the same answer as fields: `code`
(`cli_allowance_exhausted`), `message`, `scope` (`actions` or `pushes`),
`limit`, `used`, `resetsAt`, `upgradeUrl`, `reason` and `topUpUrl`.
`reason` and `topUpUrl` are `null` here; see the credits case below.

At 20% or less left, a run prints one warning on stderr, also added to
`warnings`:

```
CLI allowance: 9 of 50 publishes and pushes left this month (resets Dec 1). Upgrade: https://rive.app/pricing
```

On Voyager, a push or publish past the allowance is paid with the
Workspace's credits, the same balance the AI Agent uses (included credits
first, then top-ups). It succeeds as usual, and the CLI prints one line on
stderr in place of the warning above, also added to `warnings`:

```
Monthly CLI allowance used up, so this publish was paid with credits ($0.01). $12.34 in this Workspace's credits left. Top up: https://rive.app/pricing
```

Before sending anything, `rive push` says so too: "Monthly CLI allowance
used up, so credits will pay for pushes past it." With `--format=json`,
`credits` holds the same answer as fields: `action` (`publish`; `rive push`
prints no JSON), `spentCents` (what this run spent, in US cents),
`balanceCents` (the credits left after it) and `topUpUrl`. A number the
server did not send is `null`.

When the Workspace's credits can't pay for the next push or publish, it is
refused as above and the CLI exits 9, but the line links to topping up
instead of upgrading:

```
Monthly CLI allowance used up in Acme: 500 of 500 publishes and pushes, and the Workspace is out of credits. Top up credits or wait for the reset on Dec 1, 2026 (UTC). Top up: https://rive.app/pricing
```

In `allowance`, `reason` is then `credits` and `topUpUrl` holds the same
link. `upgradeUrl` is still there.

`rive doctor [dir]` checks the environment those commands assume: version and
pending updates, the session, the live-link port, and the project's
`rive.yaml`. It exits 1 only when a check hard-fails, and takes
`--format=json` too.

## In short

```bash
rive login                              # once, for --publish, --rev, push

rive myproject --verify                 # compile check           (no login)
rive myproject                          # live window             (no login)
rive myproject --publish                # the .riv you ship       (login)
rive myproject --rev=out.rev            # an editable .rev        (login)
rive myproject --publish=web            # host it at a url        (login)
rive myproject --list-published         # where is this published (login if web-published)
rive doctor myproject                   # is the environment sane (no login)
```

### Choosing a local export folder

Local publishing defaults to `output.dir` in `rive.yaml` (or `build`).
Use `--output-dir=<directory>` to override the folder for that invocation:

```sh
rive myproject --publish=local --output-dir=/path/to/exports
rive myproject --list-published=local --output-dir=/path/to/exports
```

Relative folders are resolved against the project directory. The `.riv` keeps
its project name, and supporting assets are written alongside it. This does not
edit `rive.yaml` or change subsequent builds. The flag also works with
`--list-published` to override the local row; it is rejected for web publishing.

In the editor's Local publish panel, **Choose folder…** opens a folder picker at
the configured output directory (or its nearest existing parent). Selecting a
folder overrides the destination for that panel; cancelling preserves it.
**Use project default** clears the selection and follows `rive.yaml` again.


## TOPIC: push

# Pushing a project to a Rive file

`rive push` builds the project and sends the result straight to a Rive file in
your workspace — no `.rev` on disk, no drag and drop. The file opens from the
editor's file browser like any other, and every push lands as a named entry in
its revision history, so any push can be inspected or restored from the
editor's revision panel.

```bash
rive login              # once per machine: same session as --publish
rive push               # build and push; the first push creates the file
```

## Starting from a file that already exists

Work that is already in Rive does not have to start over as a new project:

```bash
rive create --from-remote-file            # pick a project, then a file
rive create hero --from-remote-file=24227 # or name both
```

To find the id without a picker (an agent, or a script), list the account:

```bash
rive workspace             # the current workspace, and the ids of the others
rive workspace 408         # switch; your personal workspace until you do
rive ls                    # browse the workspace's projects (a terminal)
rive ls --plain            # the same, printed as a table
rive ls 5336               # that project: its folders, then root files
rive ls 5336 8061          # folder 8061 of project 5336
rive ls 5336 --all --json  # every file in it, one JSON object a line
rive open 24227            # open that file in the editor
```

Every row names its kind (`project`, `folder`, `file`) and its id; the JSON
keys are `projectId`, `folderId` and `fileId`, the ids the flags here take.

This downloads the file and converts it the way `--from-rev` converts a `.rev`
off disk: `scene.rml`, with every script and asset as a file laid out as the
Assets panel. The directory has to be empty or new; without one, the remote
file's name is used.

The command first tries to download the file's live content from the change log, matching
the state the editor shows. If the change log is unavailable, it receives the same live
content from the sync server, the way `rive push` does. If that fails too, it falls back to
the newest saved revision. Binary assets — images, fonts, audio — are fetched from the asset store, 
since the editor keeps their bytes outside the document itself.

The link to the file is recorded in `rive.yaml` exactly as a first push would
record it, so `rive push <dir>` sends your edits back to it, and
`rive pull <dir>` brings later editor changes down. `--from-remote-file` itself
always writes a new directory; use `pull` to refresh one that exists.

Because what you get back is meant for a push, the picker lists the projects
`rive push` lists — the ones you can write to. Naming a file id skips the
picker and pulls any file you can open, view-only projects included.

## Pulling it back down

`rive pull` is the inverse: it downloads the file the project is linked to and writes it over
the project.

A project gets that link two ways. The first `rive push` creates the file and links it, and
`rive create --from-remote-file` links the file it started from. Either way `rive pull` works
from then on, and a project with no `push:` block is told to use one of the two.

```bash
rive pull            # asks before overwriting
rive pull --yes      # skip the prompt (required in CI, an agent's shell,
                     # or anywhere with no terminal)
```

`--quiet` drops the download line and the "already matched" count, leaving only
what changed.

It rewrites the scene markup and every script, shader and asset the remote file holds, and
reports what changed:

```
downloaded 12084 bytes from changelog at 157, 3 assets
pulled file 24227 into demo
  scene.rml           updated
  ui/button.luau      updated
  images/logo.png     added
  (4 files already matched)
```

What the remote holds wins — local edits to those files are lost, which is why it asks first.
`rive.yaml` takes the remote file's main artboard, build settings and `app` block and keeps
every other line. `AGENTS.md`, `CLAUDE.md` and anything you added yourself are left alone, and a
file whose bytes already match is not rewritten at all, so an unchanged pull will not wake the
watcher.

Files that are in the project but *not* in the remote file are listed rather than deleted:
nothing can tell an asset the editor dropped from one you added on purpose. Keep the project in
source control and the whole overwrite is reviewable as a diff.

The scene markup goes into `scene.rml`. A project with several `.rml` files and no `scene.rml`
gets it in the first by path, and the pull says which in a `note:` line. Other notes say when an
asset was renamed for its file, or when an image's bytes disagree with its `format`.

Deletes in the editor don't always take what hangs off the deleted object with them, so a file
can carry content that builds into nothing. The pull reports it and changes nothing:

```
The file carries content that builds into nothing:
  55 objects attached to nothing (55 CubicEaseInterpolator)
  2 references to deleted objects, written as "0:0" (2 NestedArtboard.artboardId)
```

*Attached to nothing* is an object whose parent is gone, or an interpolator nothing uses.
Artboards, assets, view models, enums and converters whose folder was deleted still ship, so
they aren't counted. A reference to a deleted object is written as `0:0`, which builds like a reference to
nothing. Neither reaches the `.riv`, and a push sends them back as they came. A bind whose path
names a deleted view model property is a different case; `rive inspect` lists those as
`unresolved-bind-path`. `rive create --from-rev` prints the same report.

## The first push

A file lives in a folder of a project, so the first push asks where to put
it. On a terminal it opens the browser `rive ls` uses, on the projects of
the workspace you are in:

```
Rive (408)
  switch workspace…              now Rive (408)
  Personal Files/                project 2881
  Characters/                    project 5336
```

Arrows move, enter or right opens a project and then its folders, left or
backspace goes up, typing narrows the list, and escape cancels the push.
Every level offers **`choose this folder`** as its second row, and that is
what creates the file. A project's own root is a destination like any
folder, named `the project root`.

Only projects you can write to are listed, your personal files first, and
no files at all, since a file is not somewhere a file can go. A project in
another workspace is reached through `switch workspace…`, which is
remembered the way `rive ls` remembers it, so the next `rive ls`,
`rive workspace` or `rive push` starts in the new one.

Name the destination instead, and nothing is asked:

```bash
rive push --project=5336               # the project's root
rive push --project=5336 --folder=8061 # a folder in it
```

`rive ls` prints both ids, and `--folder` on its own is an error, since a
folder id alone does not say which project holds it.

Where no browser can draw, naming it is the only way through. CI, a pipe,
an agent's shell, `TERM=dumb`, `RIVE_NO_TUI=1` and a window too short all
stop with that message rather than creating somewhere you did not choose.
So does a redirect of any of the three streams, `rive push > log`
included, since a browser needs a terminal on each of them.

The new file is named after `name:` in `rive.yaml`, which `rive create` sets
to the folder's name; a blank `name:` falls back to the main artboard
(`main:`, unless it holds a path separator or colon), then to the folder's name. `--name` does not name the file: on the
first push as on every later one, it labels the push's entry in the revision
history. The first push prints both before it creates anything:

```
creating file "nSlicing", named after name: in rive.yaml (revision "N-Slicing")
```

For another file name, change `name:` before the first push (it also names
`build/<name>.riv`), or rename the file in the editor; later pushes keep
whatever name the file has.

The link to the created file is recorded in `rive.yaml`:

```yaml
push:
  projectId: 5336
  fileId: 24227
```

Commit this so everyone pushing the project updates the same file. The folder
is not recorded, since the file keeps the one it was created in.

Once the link exists, `--project` and `--folder` no longer choose anything:
the push updates the linked file wherever it lives. A `--project` naming a
different project is refused rather than ignored, so a push meant for
somewhere else can't overwrite the linked file.

To push a copy somewhere else, pass `--new-file`:

```bash
rive push --new-file --project=7120 --folder=806145
```

That creates a new file the way a first push does, and rewrites `push:` to
link the project to it, so later pushes update the copy. Without
`--project`, the new file goes in the linked project's root.

## Every push after

A push to a file the project is already linked to asks first, because it
overwrites that file:

```
Pushing rive-cli project "two_shape_lib" will overwrite remote file 37611.
Proceed? [y/N]
```

`--yes` skips it, and is required wherever nothing can answer: CI, a
redirected terminal, `RIVE_NO_TUI=1`, or an agent's shell. The first push
does not ask, since it creates the file and there is nothing to overwrite.

A later push diffs the new build against the file's live content and sends
only what differs, then names a revision. A changed object is patched in
place and keeps its id; only an object that is gone, or that changed type, is
removed. An editor with the file open drops an object's children from its
session when the object is removed, and recreating the parent does not bring
them back. `--name` labels it —
useful when a push marks something:

```bash
rive push --name="before the terrain rewrite"
```

A push with nothing new reports `already up to date` and adds no revision.
The previous content is never lost: it stays in the revision history, and the
editor can restore any entry. If someone has the file open in the editor while
you push, they see the content swap live, like a collaborator's edit — and
any editor-made changes to pushed content are overwritten, the push is
authoritative.

## Ids stay stable

Logically-same things keep their coop object ids across pushes: an asset by
its module path, an artboard (and its layout graph) by its name, folders by
their path. That matters when the pushed file is used as a library — a
consumer's reference to a library component points at an object id in this
file, and renaming *other* assets or adding new ones does not move it. Ids do
change when the thing itself is renamed or moved (it reads as a new object),
and the internal code line/run tree is renumbered whenever a source file's
text changes.

### Keep the ids in `scene.rml`

Inside an artboard, an object is matched by the `id` in your markup. After
a push, `scene.rml` holds the ids the push wrote back
([format.md](format.md#ids-and-references)). If a generator script writes
`scene.rml` again without them, the next push sees new objects: it deletes
every object and creates it again. Edit `scene.rml` in place, or have the
generator carry the ids over from the pushed file.

### Keep backups out of the project

Every `.rml` under the project folder is built, so a backup copy such as
`old/scene.rml` fails the build and the push with duplicate ids. See
[project/rive-yaml.md](project/rive-yaml.md) for the ways to keep it out.

## Sessions

Push uses the same `rive login` token as `--publish` and watermark, and so do
`rive create --from-remote-file` and `rive pull`. After the API started issuing
`cli:write` on new logins, anyone who signed in before that must run
`rive login` again — refresh does not upgrade an old token.

A 401 on `/api/me` or on opening the linked file means the session is
no longer accepted.

## What is pushed

Exactly what `--rev` would export: the project's own scripts, assets and
artboards, minus everything `excludeFromRev` drops. A library's content stays
out, because it belongs to that library's own file rather than to this one.
See [project/rive-yaml.md](project/rive-yaml.md#libraries).

## When something goes wrong

| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Not logged in` | no working session here, whether you never signed in, the token expired, or the api rejected it; run `rive login` |
| `file <id> is missing or not accessible` | the linked file was deleted or you lost access; clear `push.fileId` to create a new one |
| `not authorized for this file` | no edit permission on it, or the session is no longer accepted; try `rive login` |
| `push aborted: build failed` | fix the build first; `rive <dir> --verify` shows the problems |
| `Monthly CLI allowance used up` | the monthly CLI allowance is spent: nothing is sent, and the CLI exits 9 without retrying. A first push still creates and links the file. See [publishing.md](publishing.md#the-monthly-allowance) |
| `<dir> already contains files` | `--from-remote-file` writes a whole tree, so it wants an empty or new directory |
| `has never been saved` | the file has no content to download; open it in the editor once |
| `asset <id> download failed` | an asset the file references is not readable by your account |
| `rive-cli project "<name>" is not linked to a remote Rive file` | the project was never linked; push once, or start it with `rive create --from-remote-file` |
| `... will overwrite ... Rerun with --yes to confirm` | `push` and `pull` both ask before overwriting, and there is nobody to ask: CI, `RIVE_NO_TUI`, an agent's shell, or no terminal |
| `a first push needs somewhere to create the file` | nothing here can browse, so name it: `--project=<id>`, and `--folder=<id>` for a folder in it |
| `--folder needs the project holding it` | a folder id does not say which project it is in; pass `--project=<id>` too, or set `push.projectId` |
| `could not create a file in folder <id> of project <id>` | usually a folder of some other project; `rive ls <projectId>` lists the ones it can take |

A failed push never half-applies: content changes only land once the server
has accepted every change set, and the revision entry is added after that.


## TOPIC: publish-web

# Publishing to the web

`rive <project-dir> --publish=web` builds the project, signs it, and puts it
on the web as a page anyone can open — one url playing the built `.riv`, with
nothing to host yourself.

```bash
rive login                         # once per machine: same session as --publish
rive myproject --publish=web       # build, sign, upload, wait for it to go live
```

```
published my-scene
https://my-scene-k2f9qa.pages.rive.app
```

This is the only command that produces something a person outside your account
can look at. It is *not* the authoring preview — that is `rive <project-dir>`,
a window that rebuilds as you edit — and it is not `rive push`, which sends the
project to a Rive file in your account.

## A page belongs to a team

Pages hang off a team, never off your personal files. An account whose only
workspace is its own drafts has nowhere to publish to, and says so; create a
team in the editor, or ask to be added to one.

- with a single team, it is picked automatically
- with several, the CLI opens a picker: up and down move, typing narrows,
  enter chooses, escape backs out
- where no picker can draw (`TERM=dumb`, `RIVE_NO_TUI=1`) it falls back to a
  numbered prompt
- with stdin not a terminal, as in CI, it lists the teams and exits, so
  scripted runs stay deterministic
- `--team=<id>` skips all of that

## The name is the page

A page is identified by its name within the team. The name is lowercased into
a slug — everything outside `a-z0-9` becomes a dash — and the url is that slug
plus a short random suffix minted once, when the page is created.

Publishing the same name again **replaces what the url serves**. The url does
not change, so a link you handed out keeps working and starts showing the new
build. Publishing a different name creates a different page at a different url.
The one exception is a page that has expired; see below.

By default the name comes from the project's `name` in `rive.yaml`;
`--name=<name>` overrides it. `www`, `api`, `player`, `hosted` and `pages` are
reserved.

The binding is recorded in `rive.yaml` after the first publish:

```yaml
pages:
  teamId: 77
  name: "my-scene"
```

Only the first publish writes it, the same way `rive push` binds a file once.
Commit it, and everyone publishing the project updates the same page. A later
`--name=<name>` is a one-off — it publishes elsewhere without retargeting the
project; edit the block to move it for good, or delete it to be asked again.

## Pages can expire

On some plans a page only stays up for a while after its first publish. When
it has a date, the publish says so on its first line, in your own time zone:

```
published my-scene (expires 4 Oct)
https://my-scene-k2f9qa.pages.rive.app
```

Republishing a live page keeps its date. Once a page has expired, its url
stays offline and its name frees up, so publishing the name again makes a
**new page at a new url**.

## Waiting, or not

The upload returns before the page is live: the api hands the work to a
background job, and the CLI polls it. Until the job finishes, the url keeps
serving whatever it served before — a republish never leaves the page broken
in between.

`--no-wait` prints the url and exits as soon as the upload is accepted, which
is what a CI job that does not need the confirmation wants. With `--quiet`,
stdout is two lines, the name (and its expiry, if it has one) and then the
url:

```bash
url=$(rive myproject --publish=web --no-wait --quiet | tail -1)
```

What `--list-published=web` can tell you afterwards is narrower than it
looks: it reports `publishing` until a page's *first* publish finishes and
`published` from then on, including while a republish is still running. So it
answers "has this page ever gone live", not "did the publish I just started
land". For that, open the url.

## The page's controls

A published page carries a small bar of controls, for its fit, full screen
and copying its url, that shows for a moment and then hides to a lip at the
bottom of the page. `--drawer=<mode>` changes how it starts:

| Mode | The page |
|---|---|
| `docked` | keeps the bar out |
| `hidden` | starts with just the lip |
| `none` | has no bar at all (paid plans) |

The first time the bar opens, a tooltip over its Rive link reads "Made with
Rive. Build your own." for a few seconds. A page that starts as just the lip
shows it above the lip first. `--no-promo` leaves it off (paid plans).

Each publish sends its own mode and promo setting, so one without `--drawer=`
or `--no-promo` goes back to the default; pass them every time, the same way
as `--no-wait`. Visitors can still dock, hide or remove the bar whatever the
page starts with.

## Listing and taking down

```bash
rive myproject --list-published            # where is this project published?
rive myproject --list-published=web        # every live page on the team, with its url
rive myproject --unpublish=web             # take the project's page down
rive myproject --unpublish=web --name=prototype   # by name, or by the full page id
```

```
  my-scene   published   https://my-scene-k2f9qa.pages.rive.app
  prototype  publishing  https://prototype-8h2mza.pages.rive.app
```

`publishing` is a page whose *first* publish has not finished; a page that has
been live once reads `published` even mid-republish. `--unpublish=web` asks
first unless `--yes` is passed, and there is no undo: the url stops resolving,
the files are removed, and the name frees up. Publishing that name again mints
a *new* url — the old link does not come back.

### Where is this project published?

`--list-published` (no target) prints one row per target, `local` then `web`,
so it always answers something even for a project that has never gone
anywhere:

```bash
rive myproject --list-published
```

```
  local  built          myproject/build/hello_rive.riv
  web    not published
```

`built` means the file is on disk, not that it is signed: a project with no
scripts publishes an unsigned `.riv`, and an older CLI may have written one
with `--once`.

`web` reads `not published` when there is no page to read: either the project
has no `pages:` binding in `rive.yaml`, or the page that binding names is not
among the team's. A page that *is* found reports its own state instead —
`publishing` while its first publish is still running, `published` once it is
live — so `not published` means no page was found, never a page mid-publish.

When the web row cannot be determined, it prints `unknown` instead:

```
  local  built    myproject/build/hello_rive.riv
  web    unknown
```

The reason is printed on stderr. The command exits 0 if every row is determined,
or with one of the following codes if any row is `unknown` or if an error occurs:

| Exit | Reason |
|---|---|
| 0 | every row determined |
| 1 | most failures: forbidden (403), permission denied, rate limited (429), server errors, or anything unexpected; also when the directory is not a Rive project |
| 3 | not logged in, or the stored login was rejected; also network failures while renewing an expired token |
| 7 | after login is established, a service could not be reached — safe to retry |

A project with no `pages:` binding exits 0 even if the web service is unreachable,
because there is nothing to determine — it is certainly not published.

`--list-published=web` works outside a project directory as long as
`--team=<id>` is passed; `--unpublish=web` also requires `--name=<name>`.
Bare `--list-published` does not — it needs the project, because the project
is the thing being asked about.

## Scripts are signed

A page is played by a web runtime, and web runtimes refuse unsigned scripts —
an unsigned build would load and then play nothing. So `--publish=web`
always builds the way `--publish` does: scripts compiled and signed
server-side, which is why it needs a session even for a project you could
otherwise build offline.

The same watermark rule applies as `--publish`. A project with no `push.fileId`
in `rive.yaml` has nothing for the API to attribute the publish to and is
watermarked whatever the plan; `rive push` binds the project to a file and
takes the watermark off. See [publishing.md](publishing.md).

## When something goes wrong

| Message | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `Not logged in` | no working session here, whether you never signed in, the token expired, or the api rejected it; run `rive login` |
| `no team to publish to` | the account has no team, only personal files |
| `no team to publish to: check --team=<id>` | the team id is wrong, or you are no longer a member |
| `publish aborted: build failed` | fix the build first; `rive <dir> --verify` shows the problems. When another line from this table follows it, that line is the reason |
| `"<name>" is reserved` | pick another `--name` |
| `Invalid page name` | the api refused the slug; usually too long |
| `publish failed: Upload missing` | the upload did not survive to the job; publish again |
| `too many publishes for now` | the per-account rate limit for publishing; the message names the wait when the api does |
| `This workspace's plan allows <n> hosted pages` | the plan's page limit; take a page down with `--unpublish=web`, or upgrade |
| `Pages on this workspace's plan show the Rive promo` (or `show the drawer`) | `--no-promo` and `--drawer=none` need a paid plan; nothing was published |
| `Monthly CLI allowance used up` | the monthly CLI allowance is spent; nothing was published, the CLI exits 9 and does not retry. The line names the reset date and the upgrade link (the top-up link when the Workspace is out of credits). A web publish counts once, as a publish |
| `You need edit access to this file to publish it from the CLI` | you're a Viewer on the file in `push.fileId`; ask an admin of its Workspace for edit access. Nothing was uploaded, exit 1 |
| `the publish has not finished after 300s` | the job is stuck or slow; open the url to see what the page is serving |
| `deleting a page stops its url resolving; rerun with --yes` | no terminal to confirm on: CI, `RIVE_NO_TUI`, or stdin not a tty |
| `your role on that team cannot see its pages` | you lack read permission on that team (applies to `--list-published`, `--list-published=web`) |
| `too many requests for now` | read rate limited; the message names the wait when the api does (applies to `--list-published`, `--list-published=web`) |
| `--team= applies to --publish=web, --unpublish=web and --list-published=web` (or `--name=`, `--drawer=`, `--no-promo`, `--no-wait`, `--yes`) | that flag does not apply to the publish mode you asked for |
| `unknown drawer "<mode>"; use docked, hidden or none` | `--drawer=` takes only those; nothing was built or uploaded |
| `--optimize and --define= apply to a build, not to --unpublish or --list-published` | those tune a build, and neither of those commands builds anything |
| `page listing has no pages array` | the api answered 200 with something that is not a page listing; usually a proxy or a sign-in portal answering in its place, so check the network before the CLI |

Publishes are rate limited per account — a few an hour is fine, a build loop
publishing on every save is not.

`--list-published=web` needs only view access on the team; `--publish=web`
and `--unpublish=web` need write.
